chapter1.title: Chapter 1: The Birth of a Legend

sections.title: Section One: The Birth of a Necessity
sections.content:
A World of Wire and Iron

Imagine an engineer in 1968. Not a purchasing manager, not an accountant; a design engineer sitting behind a desk covered in component catalogs. His mission: building the controller for a new machine for the factory. For instance, an automatic counting and packaging system.

Until yesterday, the previous version of this machine had been built with a few hundred TTL chips and thousands of hand-soldered wires. Today, the factory manager has ordered that the new machine must be twice as fast, have more memory, and print a daily report. Our engineer looks at the design he drew last month and knows he must start everything from scratch. The old board is useless. Wired logic, like a line carved into stone, cannot be changed. He must design a new board, with a fresh arrangement of chips, and again, if a new requirement comes tomorrow, this board too will join the scrap heap of history.

This was the real nightmare of the electronics industry in the 1960s:
Disposable logic. Each new product demanded new hardware. Every small change in functionality meant a redesign of the printed circuit board, rewiring, and months of testing. The cost of designing custom hardware for every application was bound to the feet of innovation like a great stone.

On a larger scale, the makers of big computers were grappling with another version of the same disease. Each new model from DEC or IBM had its own unique internal architecture. But their main problem was not software incompatibility – that was the customer's pain, not the maker's. The makers' own problem was the same as that of the factory controller engineer: designing new hardware for each generation, on a massive scale and with astronomical cost. Chaining the customer to a closed ecosystem was a side effect of this situation, not its root cause.

In the heart of Fairchild Semiconductor, a spark was taking shape. A young engineer named Ted Hoff, who worked on memory chip design, had grown sick of this broken cycle. In conversation with his colleague Stanley Mazor, he put forward an idea that seemed naive at first glance: "Instead of scattering the logic of computation across dozens of chips, why not gather it all into one chip? A central chip that could play the role of the brain for any device by executing different instructions?"

Hoff's idea was the separation of "operational logic" from "physical hardware." Instead of designing a dedicated electronic board with fixed wiring for each product, a standard chip could play any role by reading instructions stored in memory. Today a packaging controller, tomorrow a calculator, the day after a fire alarm system. The hardware stayed the same; it was the software that changed.

The idea went nowhere at Fairchild. But destiny had another plan.

In 1969, the Japanese company Busicom placed an order with Intel – which had just broken away from Fairchild – to design a set of twelve custom chips for an advanced calculator. Ted Hoff, now at Intel, instead of following the original plan, made a revolutionary proposal to Busicom: instead of twelve chips, let us design four. One of them would be a central processing unit that performed all calculations. By changing the program stored in memory, the same hardware could do different tasks.

Busicom's managers, after a brief hesitation, accepted. And that is how the work began.

Hoff and Mazor designed the logical architecture on paper. But turning this design into a real chip on silicon was a task of miraculous proportion. This is where two decisive people entered the story: Federico Faggin, an Italian engineer who had just joined Intel and was the unrivaled master of physical chip design; and Masatoshi Shima, a Japanese engineer from Busicom who implemented the digital logic with obsessive precision. Faggin later said: "Without Shima, the 4004 would never have been built." This four-man team – Hoff, Mazor, Shima, and Faggin – were the ones who brought the world's first commercial microprocessor to fruition.

On November 15, 1971, the Intel 4004 was introduced: a 4-bit chip with 2,300 transistors. On the surface, just a faster brain for advanced calculators. But at its core, it carried a revolutionary concept: universal programmable control. For the first time, "what the device does" had been separated from "its physical wiring."

Over the months that followed, creative engineers in corners around the world discovered this concept. In big cities, traffic light controllers that were once panels full of relays and wires now worked with one 4004 and one memory chip. Changing the traffic pattern no longer required dispatching an engineering team and rewiring; it was enough to replace the memory chip with one that had a new program. This was a quiet, silent revolution that was unfolding in medical devices, industrial controllers, and security systems.

sections.title: Section Two: A Bridge Toward the Personal Computer
sections.content:
The 4004 had a fundamental limitation: it processed only 4 bits in one cycle. In a world where the standard for text processing was 8-bit ASCII codes, this was like walking on one leg. The industry needed a processor that could process a full "byte" all at once.

Intel answered in April 1972 with the 8008: the world's first 8-bit microprocessor. The story of the 8008's birth held an important lesson within it. The company CTC (later Datapoint) wanted to build a desktop computer for small businesses: the Datapoint 2200. They approached Intel for the processor design, and their needs directly shaped the architecture of the 8008. Intel built the 8008 to be the beating heart of that computer.

But destiny once again charted a different path. The first samples of the 8008 arrived late, and their performance – due to the use of slow PMOS technology – was unsatisfactory. CTC's engineers, tired of waiting, built their machine with around a hundred discrete TTL chips and cast the 8008 aside. Thus, the first attempt to build a personal computer based on a microprocessor met with relative failure.

But the 8008 taught the industry a great lesson: an 8-bit microprocessor, conceptually, could be the core of a complete computer. The path was open.

The lessons of the 4004 and the 8008 – one a victory, the other a semi-failure – led Intel to design a processor that changed everything. In April 1974, the Intel 8080 came to market: faster NMOS technology, 2 MHz clock speed, and a rich instruction set. But the true genius of the 8080 was not in its hardware; it was in Intel's open approach. They published complete documentation and explicitly invited other companies to build compatible peripheral chips. This move created a large market of memories, controllers, and input/output ports, all revolving around the 8080.

The fruit of this open ecosystem ripened in January 1975. Popular Electronics magazine unveiled a device called the Altair 8800 on its cover: a computer based on the 8080, offered as a kit for $439. The reaction was beyond imagination. Tens of thousands of orders poured in from engineers, students, and enthusiasts who had never before had access to a computer.

The Altair became the birthplace of a social movement. In garages and basements, users built hardware for it and shared designs in magazines like BYTE. Two young students named Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote a BASIC interpreter for the Altair – and this became the cornerstone of a small company called Micro-Soft.

But the Altair's most important legacy was what Gary Kildall created. Kildall, a quiet university professor with a PhD in computer science, wrote an operating system called CP/M. The genius of CP/M was this: a standard software layer that sat between application programs and different hardware. A programmer could write a word processor like WordStar once and be sure it would run on any machine that had CP/M.

Thus, CP/M rapidly became the governing standard for business computers. And this created a massive strategic asset for the 8080 architecture: a vast library of business software that practically only ran on 8080-compatible processors. Now it was no longer hardware that sold the computer; it was software. Companies bought computers to run WordStar and VisiCalc. Any processor that wanted to be taken seriously in the market had to conquer this software territory.

sections.title: Section Three: A Different Vision and a Rebellion from Pennsylvania
sections.content:
As the 8080 conquered the market, a completely different vision was offered by Motorola: the 6800 processor. If the 8080 was the symbol of an open and sometimes chaotic ecosystem, the 6800 was the embodiment of order, integration, and engineering elegance.

Motorola's team, led by Tom Bennett – who had seen the initial idea from Ted Hoff – insisted on different principles. The 6800 needed only a single +5V power supply, while the 8080 required three different voltages. This simplicity meant lower cost, higher reliability, and easier power supply design. The internal architecture of the 6800 was also symmetrical and logical, making its assembly programming intuitive and less error-prone. But most importantly, there was Motorola's "system on chip" approach: they offered the 6800 not as a lone chip, but as the central core of the "M6800 family" – a complete set of memory and interface chips that worked naturally together.

Federico Faggin, the architect of the 8080, confessed with respect: "The 6800 has a better architecture. It is a more orderly machine."

But the 6800 had two weaknesses: a higher price, and the absence of the massive software ecosystem that the 8080 had inherited from CP/M. Motorola never conquered the personal computer market, but it remained unrivaled elsewhere: industry. Point-of-sale terminals, early ATMs, and industrial controllers – where durability and reliability mattered more than raw processing power – became the undisputed territory of the 6800.

Now the market had two powerful poles: Intel with a massive software ecosystem but relatively complex hardware, and Motorola with beautiful, integrated design but expensive and lacking in business software. It was as if the industry awaited a synthesis of the two.

But before that, an earthquake from Pennsylvania caught everyone by surprise.

Chuck Peddle, a self-taught engineer and former soldier with a rebellious spirit, was one of the designers of the 6800 at Motorola. When Motorola's management kept the price of the 6800 high, Peddle could not bear it. He told his colleague Bill Mensch: "They think a processor is a luxury commodity. But I know that this is the building block of the future. It must be so cheap that every schoolchild can buy one."

Peddle and Mensch left Motorola in the spring of 1974 and joined a small, obscure company called MOS Technology in Pennsylvania. There, in a windowless room, on a meager budget, they began working. Peddle led stormy brainstorming sessions with shouts: "Cut this part! What does the customer really want? Cheapness and efficiency!" Mensch, silent and focused, drew the new architecture with minimal transistors on paper.

The result was unveiled in September 1975 at the Atlantic City exhibition: the MOS 6502. Price? $25. While the 8080 cost around $175.

A wave of shock, then excitement, swept through the hall. Young engineers surrounded the MOS booth. One of them was Steve Wozniak, who bought a few samples and built a computer with them in his parents' garage. His friend Steve Jobs insisted on selling it. They named it the Apple I – and this was the spark that built Apple. Later, Commodore placed the 6502 in the heart of the best-selling personal computer in history, the Commodore 64, and the Atari 2600 game console.

Peddle had proven that low price was itself a form of power. But the 6502 was not compatible with the 8080 – this processor belonged to a parallel world, the world of consumers and games, not the business market under CP/M's rule. Kildall's software empire still remained untouched.

sections.title: Section Four: Coup in the Shadows
sections.content:
In Federico Faggin's office at Intel, the atmosphere was heavy. He was the architect of the 4004 and the 8080, a man in whose veins flowed the dust of silicon. He had come from Italy to live the dream of building integrated circuits, and now his greatest achievement – the 8080 – had conquered the market.

But Intel's management, led by Gordon Moore and Andy Grove, saw the future differently. Their strategy was focused on semiconductor memories, and they considered the microprocessor a side activity. They refused to invest seriously in the next generation.

Faggin was enraged by this shortsightedness. In the fall of 1974, he made his decision. He went to Ralph Ungermann, an intelligent and ambitious executive, and in a simple restaurant in Palo Alto said: "Ralph, we are building the future, but they only see the past. I want to build a company that is focused on only one thing: building the world's best microprocessor. Not good – the best."

Ungermann accepted. With investment from the oil company Exxon, Zilog was founded in November 1974. Its name was derived from "Z-integrated logic," and the Z, the last letter of the alphabet, seemed to signify a will to build the final and ultimate processor.

But Faggin was not alone. He went to Masatoshi Shima. Shima, the brilliant Japanese engineer who had built the 8080 architecture alongside Faggin, was now in Japan. Faggin sat across from him in a Japanese restaurant and said without preamble: "Shima-san, we want to complete what we started with the 8080. A processor that is not just better than the 8080, but better than anything that exists. You must come with us." Shima, without the slightest hesitation, bowed his head in agreement.

The golden circle was complete: Faggin, Shima, and Ungermann. Three men with three complementary forces: vision, precision, and management. They gathered in Zilog's small office in Cupertino and put on paper three principles that would change the course of history:

1. Full Compatibility: The new processor had to be binary-compatible with the 8080. All of that CP/M software empire – WordStar, dBASE, and whatever came later – had to run on the new chip without the smallest change. This was an inheritance that could not be ignored.
2. Absolute Superiority: They must not just build a faster 8080. They had to advance in everything: more registers, more powerful instructions, higher speed, and – the great lesson of the 6800 – a single +5V power supply. The new processor had to have the best of both worlds at once: the power of the 8080 ecosystem, and the engineering elegance of the 6800.
3. A Price to Shock the Market: Not so low as to enter a fruitless war with the 6502 in the consumer market (the CP/M business market was the target, not game consoles), but competitive enough to tempt 8080 and 8085 customers at Intel to migrate.

The year 1976 began. On the surface, everything in the industry was calm. Intel was working on the 8085 – an attempt to bring single-voltage power supply to the 8080 architecture, designed precisely to counter the 6800's advantage. Motorola still relied on the elegant but expensive 6800. MOS was devouring the consumer market with the 6502. And the CP/M empire, with unshakable loyalty to the 8080 architecture, ruled over the world of business software.

But in Zilog's office, the silence meant nothing but pure concentration. Faggin and Shima were bent over silicon blueprints day and night. They had only one chance, and they knew it.

On a spring evening in March 1976, Faggin finished the final review. He rose from his desk, went to the window, and stared at the empty street beyond the glass. Then, he turned to Shima and his small team and said with a calmness that came from certainty: "It is finished. We have it."

He paused, and then, with a voice slightly louder: "Now they must know that a new king has come."

The Z80 was now born. And nothing would ever be the same again.

sections.title: Section One: The Inheritance That Must Not Burn
sections.content:
By the end of March 1976, the Z80 had emerged from the design phase and, like a fetus that has taken its first heartbeat, was breathing on the test bench in Los Altos. But the path this chip had traveled until that moment was not just nine months and a budget of four hundred thousand dollars. It was a path that had passed through the failures, the lessons, and the wounds of the two previous generations of microprocessors.

Faggin had felt this path with his own flesh and bone. He was there when the 4004 was born from the heart of a calculator order and no one but himself, Shima, and Hoff knew what genie had come out of the bottle. He was there when the 8080 conquered the market but simultaneously chained the feet of engineers: three different voltages, a mandatory external clock generator, and an instruction set that, though revolutionary for its time, was now falling short. And he was a spectator when Motorola's 6800 arrived and showed what advantage a clean and integrated architecture had, but its high price and lack of business software prevented it from conquering the big market.

Now the Z80 had to digest all these lessons at once. It could not just be a faster 8080. It could not just imitate the 6800. And it could not, like the 6502, sacrifice everything for a low price. The Z80 had to be something no one had built until that day: a complete synthesis.

The Magic of Silicon – Z80 Architecture Under the Magnifying Glass

Let us take a step back and think about what a processor in 1976 really was. Today a modern chip has billions of transistors. The Z80 had only eight thousand five hundred transistors. For comparison, the 8080 had four thousand eight hundred, and the 6800 had four thousand one hundred. With this limited number, Shima and Faggin had to resort to a kind of engineering magic to fit everything they had in mind onto a rectangle of silicon measuring roughly four by four millimeters.

Dual Registers: A Puzzle Solved with One EXX

Imagine you are in a busy kitchen cooking dinner. On the front counter, chopped ingredients are laid out: onion, garlic, herbs, meat. Suddenly the phone rings. In an ordinary kitchen, you must gather all the ingredients, set them aside, answer the phone, and then return and lay everything out again from scratch.

Registers in a processor are exactly this front counter. The data currently being processed are kept right there. The 8080 had seven of these counters. The 6800 had only two. The 6502 had three.

When an interrupt occurred – for example, a user pressed a key, or data arrived from a disk – the processor had to suspend the current work, send the contents of the registers one by one to memory (which was slow and costly), handle the interrupt, and then restore everything. This process could take tens of clock cycles.

Shima offered a brilliant yet simple solution: two complete rows of counters. One for current work, the other for emergencies. They named them shadow registers. The first set included BC, DE, HL, AF. The second set held BC', DE', HL', AF'. The apostrophe was the mark of the "backup version."

Now when an interrupt came, it was enough to execute one instruction: EXX. Just four clock cycles. And all the contents of the first row were swapped with the second row. As if you had exchanged the entire kitchen with one click. No shuttling back and forth to memory, no waste of time. Engineers working on real-time systems – industrial controllers, medical equipment, telephone routers – saw this feature not as a luxury option, but as a vital necessity.

But Faggin went one step further. He designed a separate instruction for swapping only the AF registers with AF': EX AF, AF'. Why? Because the Flags were kept in the F register – bits that showed whether the result of the last operation was zero, negative, or had overflowed. Sometimes you only needed to save the state of the flags, not everything. The Z80 let you do exactly what you needed, nothing more and nothing less.

sections.title: Section Two: IX and IY, and the Revolution in Memory Operations
sections.content:
IX and IY: Mapping the City of Data

Imagine you are in a large library looking for a book. Your desired shelf is row 12, tier 3, and the fourth book from the left. Now if the library has a system that says "start from shelf 12, then go to tier 3, then take the fourth book," your work becomes simple. You do not need to calculate the exact address of the shelf from zero every time.

Index Registers do exactly this. You place a base address in them – for example, the start of a table or an array – and then with a small number called an offset, you access any point in that table.

Motorola's 6800 had one index register and this single feature made programming data structures far simpler than the 8080. The 8080 had no index register at all. To access the nth element of an array, you had to put the start address in HL, load the value n separately, add them together, and then go to that address. A programming nightmare.

The Z80 brought two index registers: IX and IY. Two, not one. Why two? Because in real programs, you often deal with two data structures simultaneously: one array for input, one for output. Or one table for searching, and one buffer for storing results. With IX and IY, you had both available at the same time.

Shima designed complete instructions for these registers. You could work with 8-bit offsets (from -128 to +127). You could load any of the 8-bit registers into the location pointed to by IX, or vice versa. You could perform arithmetic operations directly on data sitting at the address IX+offset. This level of flexibility existed in no other 8-bit processor.

Revolution in Memory Operations: LDIR and CPIR

Now think of one of the most tedious programming tasks in the 8080: copying a block of a hundred bytes of memory from one place to another. In the 8080 you had to write something like this:

LOOP:   MOV A,M    ; take the byte from address HL
        STAX D     ; put it at address DE
        INX H      ; advance HL by one
        INX D      ; advance DE by one
        DCR C      ; decrement the counter
        JNZ LOOP   ; if not finished, go back

Five instructions that together formed a loop. A hundred bytes meant these five instructions had to execute a hundred times.

The Z80 had just one instruction: LDIR. Short for LoaD, Increment, Repeat. One instruction. One line of code. The processor itself knew how many times to do this (the count was stored in BC), it advanced the addresses itself, and it knew when to stop.

CPIR was similar, but for searching: ComPare, Increment, Repeat. Looking for a specific byte among thousands of bytes? One instruction was enough. It was as if the Z80 had a built-in search engine.

These block instructions did not just save the programmer's time. They also dramatically increased speed. Because the loop ran inside the processor itself, there was no repeated shuttling to memory to read instructions. Zilog's engineers calculated that LDIR for large blocks operated up to four times faster than its 8080 equivalent.

Bit Operations: Surgery on Individual Bits

In the 8080, if you wanted to set the third bit of a register to one, what did you have to do? You would make a mask (for example, 00001000), logically OR it with the register, and return the result. Several instructions, and in the meantime, you also had to save the previous contents of the register somewhere.

The Z80 had a complete set of bit instructions: BIT (test a bit), SET (set a bit to one), RES (reset a bit to zero). Each could be executed on any bit of any 8-bit register. You could even execute them directly on data sitting at an IX or IY address, without first moving it to a register.

For programming industrial control systems, this was as essential as daily bread. Imagine a sensor connected to an input port reporting the status of eight different devices in one byte. Bit 3 relates to the furnace temperature. With the Z80 you could directly say: BIT 3, A. If bit 3 was on, the furnace was hot. No mask, no intermediate operations.

sections.title: Section Three: Relative Jumps, Refresh Register, and the Interrupt System
sections.content:
Relative Jumps: Code That Carried Itself

In the 8080, all jumps were absolute. That is, you had to write the exact address of the destination in the code. If you wanted to say "if the result was zero, go ten bytes forward," you had to calculate where exactly ten bytes forward would be in memory. This meant your code was dependent on its location in memory. Programs were "hard" – they could not easily be relocated.

The Z80 brought the JR instruction: Jump Relative. Instead of an absolute address, you gave a small signed number (from -128 to +127). "If zero, go forward 10." "If not, go back 5." Now the program could be loaded anywhere in memory and still work correctly. This feature was vital for an operating system like CP/M that had to load programs at different memory addresses.

The R Register: The Soldier Who Also Washed the Dishes

And now we come to perhaps the Z80's most clever trick: the R register or Refresh Register.

DRAM memories, which rapidly gained popularity in the 1970s, worked based on tiny capacitors that held electrical charge – charged meaning 1, empty meaning 0. But these capacitors lost their charge within a few milliseconds. Like a bucket that leaked. To prevent data from vanishing, every memory cell had to be regularly read and rewritten. This was called Refresh.

In 8080-based systems, a separate circuit on the board had to perform this task. This circuit added extra cost, took up space, and was itself a potential source of failure. The situation was the same in the 6800 and 6502.

Faggin thought: the processor itself is constantly accessing memory. Why not use these same accesses for Refresh? The R register was a 7-bit counter that increased by one with every instruction fetch from memory. Its upper seven bits – which were constantly changing – were connected to the upper address lines of the bus, and in this way, all rows of DRAM memory were automatically and continuously refreshed.

The beauty of this solution was that it was completely free. The processor was accessing memory anyway. Refresh was just a byproduct of these accesses. It required no extra hardware, no extra software, not even an extra clock cycle.

For system builders, this meant eliminating an entire chip from the board. Lower cost, less complexity, higher reliability. The Z80 alone did the work that previously required two chips. This silent integration was perhaps more important than all its new instructions, because it directly affected the final price of the product.

The Invisible Arsenal – Interrupts

The Z80's architecture had another hidden layer that fit in no table: interrupts.

The 8080 had a simple interrupt system. When an external device wanted the processor's attention, it sent a signal. The processor stopped its current work and jumped to a fixed address. Only one type of interrupt, only one address.

The Z80 had three interrupt modes:

Mode 0: Exactly like the 8080. For full compatibility.

Mode 1: The simplest mode. An interrupt occurred and the processor jumped to address 0038h. For very simple systems that had only one interrupting device.

Mode 2: And this was the real magic. In this mode, the external device placed an 8-bit vector on the data bus. The Z80 combined this vector with the contents of the I register (another 8-bit register that you had preset) and formed a 16-bit address. It then went to that address, read a 16-bit word, and jumped to the address contained in that word.

The result: you could have 128 different devices, each with its own interrupt, and each with its own separate service routine. The Z80 had a complete vectored interrupt system without needing any external interrupt controller. For computers dealing with disk drives, printers, keyboards, and serial ports, this was a blessing.

And one more thing: the I register we mentioned supplied the upper eight bits of the interrupt address. But the lower seven bits of the R register could also be used for Refresh. The Z80 had combined these two to give maximum functionality with minimal hardware. This kind of optimization was Shima's signature.

sections.title: Section Four: The Battle in the Market and Beyond the Iron Curtain
sections.content:
The Battle in the Market – 1976 to 1978

By the end of 1976, the Z80 had transformed from an engineering project into a real product. But selling a processor is different from selling an ordinary commodity. You must bring an entire ecosystem along with you: hardware makers who will design their boards around your processor, programmers who will write code for it, and customers who are willing to accept the risk of migrating from an established platform.

The Z80 had one great trump card: CP/M. Gary Kildall, the creator of this operating system, quickly recognized the Z80's potential. CP/M not only ran on the Z80, but thanks to the new instructions, it ran faster too. Kildall optimized a version of CP/M for the Z80, and this meant that all of that vast library of business software – WordStar, dBASE II, SuperCalc, and dozens of other programs – was available for the Z80 overnight.

The first commercial computer with the Z80 was built by Cromemco. Roger Melen, Cromemco's founder, was one of those early customers who came to Zilog's office and bought two chips. Cromemco's Z-1 was released in late 1976 and, though its price was high ($2,495), it proved that the Z80 worked in a real product.

But the main wave was launched by another company: Radio Shack.

The TRS-80, released in August 1977 at a price of $599, placed the Z80 at its heart. Radio Shack had five thousand stores across America and the TRS-80 quickly became the best-selling personal computer of the years 1977 to 1979. The Z80 was no longer just an interesting chip for engineers; it was becoming a household name.

That same year, Japanese companies that had previously only watched joined the line. NEC took an official license for the Z80 and began making its own version: the μPD780. Toshiba, Sharp, and Hitachi followed suit. The Z80 was becoming a global standard.

Meanwhile, Intel had released the 8085 and was trying to recapture the market. The 8085 had lowered its price to $30 in volume and in terms of pure price, it was cheaper than the Z80. But it was already too late. The CP/M ecosystem was now practically optimized for the Z80. Computer makers preferred to pay ten dollars more for the processor and in return have access to all that software, rather than buy cheaper and be deprived of the software.

In the technical documentation of 1978, industry analysts wrote that the Z80 had captured more than sixty percent of the 8-bit desktop processor market. This number was unbelievable for an eleven-person company that was only two years old.

Beyond the Iron Curtain

And then, a strange thing happened. The Z80 crossed beyond the borders of the Western world.

In the Soviet Union, processors were not just electronic components. They were strategic goods whose export to the Eastern Bloc was under strict control. But the Russians wanted the Z80 – and they found their own way to reach it.

They obtained samples of the Z80 from the open market, chemically stripped the layers, extracted the design, and built their own version. The result was a processor with the code KP580IK80 (which, incidentally, had the number 80 in its code referring to the 8080, not the Z80 – a sign that they too had started from the 8080 but ultimately copied the Z80 architecture). This Soviet version had minor changes: the maximum frequency was limited to 2.5 MHz (instead of the original Z80's 4 MHz), and some peripheral features were removed. But in essence, it was the same Z80.

The countries of the Eastern Bloc – East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Romania – all built their own versions of the Z80. In East Germany, the Microelectronics Combine Erfurt produced the U880 processor, which remained in production until the fall of the Berlin Wall. Interestingly, the U880 was in some respects better than the early Z80 samples – it tolerated higher frequencies and consumed less power.

The Z80 had become the processor that knew no walls. Not the walls of commercial competition, not the walls of engineering, and not even the Berlin Wall.

End of the Chapter

By late 1978, less than three years after the founding of Zilog, the Z80 had become an empire. From business computers in New York offices to industrial controllers in Stuttgart factories, from game consoles in Tokyo (yes, the Z80 was the beating heart of many arcade machines) to military equipment on both sides of the Iron Curtain.

Faggin had reached what he wanted: the Z80 was the undisputed king of the 8-bit world. But he was smart enough to know that this reign would not last forever. On the horizon, a storm was coming: the 16-bit world. Intel introduced the 8086 in June 1978. Motorola's 68000 arrived in 1979. Zilog itself designed the Z8000 – a 16-bit processor that, though it did not achieve the success of the Z80, showed that Faggin and his team had their eyes on the future.

But that is the story of the third chapter. For now, at this moment in history, in late 1978, the Z80 sat on the throne. The processor that three rebels had built with a meager budget and an eleven-person team was now pulsing the heartbeat of millions of devices around the world. And it was going to keep pulsing for another fifty years.

chapter3.title: Chapter 3: Conquering the Market in the West

sections.title: Section One: The Battle with Intel and Motorola
sections.content:
March 1976. The same month the first Z80 samples came out of Zilog's production line, Intel sent another chip to market: the 8085.

The number "5" in the name of Intel's new chip had a special meaning. This number told the customer: "We have removed the three damn voltages. Now only 5 volts is enough." The very thing Motorola's 6800 had done from the start and the very thing the Z80 was doing too.

Intel had seen and understood what advantage Motorola's single-voltage had. It had understood that the Z80 was entering with that very same trump card. But it had moved too late. The Z80 was already four months ahead of the 8085.

The 8085, however, had taken one correct step in terms of hardware. Now it needed one voltage to operate, not three. The clock generator was also housed inside the chip. There was no more of all that extra wiring.

But elsewhere, it repeated the same crooked steps. It still had seven registers. It still had no more than 78 instructions. It still did not know how to do DRAM Refresh. To build a computer with the 8085, extra circuits were still needed. The final cost still came out higher than the Z80. And one more important thing: it was slower than the Z80.

---

On the other side of the field stood Motorola with the 6800.

A beautiful chip, orderly, academic. A single-voltage power supply that from the very beginning of its work was one of its winning cards. Motorola's engineers in 1974, two years before the Z80, had thought that 5 volts was enough. Intel learned this lesson late, but Zilog learned it from the start.

But the 6800 had only two general-purpose registers. Its instruction set was limited. 72 instructions, against the Z80's 158 instructions. And programming with it was not simple. Each instruction accepted only a few specific addressing modes. The programmer had to memorize which instruction worked with which method. He was constantly forced to consult the manual.

And its price was 175 dollars. Against the Z80's 70 dollars in high volume. More than double the cost for a system that also had fewer features.

Motorola did not sit silent. It sent improved versions, the 6802 and 6808, to market. But it did not make much difference. The 6800 architecture might be "more beautiful," but in the market, beauty does not always win. Sometimes "good enough and cheap enough" wins. And the Z80 had exactly these features, and the market needed exactly this.

---

But let us see what the market really wanted.

In the fall of 1975, a year before the Z80's introduction, the Homebrew Computer Club in Silicon Valley conducted a survey. It asked its members: what processor do you use? The result: 25 people used the 8080, 9 people the 6800, 7 people the 6502.

Six months later, in the spring of 1976, they surveyed again. This time, the Z80 was also on the list. No one was using it yet. But the 8080 had risen to 37 users, the 6800 remained at the same 9. And the 6502 had not increased beyond 7.

Three months later, in the summer of 1976, the Z80 was introduced. In the next survey, two people were already using it. This processor had just arrived, but it had finally found customers.

The year 1978, two years later. Researchers from the University of Southern California conducted a new survey at two Los Angeles computer shows. Of the 267 people who responded, 231 already had a personal computer, and their total computers numbered 366.

Of these 366 machines, 108 worked with the 8080 and 107 with the Z80!

That is, 215 machines out of 366, or 59 percent, used the 8080 and Z80 family. And this just two years after the Z80's introduction.

Victory belonged to Zilog. But the battle was not only over hardware. The main battle was raging somewhere else.

---

On the calm coast of California, in Monterey, a man sat behind a desk, and in front of him was a computer with an 8080 processor. A newly arrived and strange eight-inch floppy drive and a big problem.

His name was Gary Kildall. A computer science professor at the Naval Postgraduate School.

His problem was this: every computer maker had its own method for reading and writing to disk. A program that worked on company A's machine would not run at all on company B's machine. Kildall was tired of this chaos.

In 1973, he sat behind his desk and began to write. He named the program CP/M. Short for Control Program for Microcomputers.

A software layer that sat between the program and the hardware. It told the programmer: "You just write your code. I will worry about the disk, the printer, and the memory."

By 1976, CP/M had been installed on thousands of computers. Thousands. Any company that built a business computer either had to get permission from Kildall, or had to write an operating system that could talk to CP/M.

And that very same year, the Z80 arrived. With one simple promise: "Whatever has been written for the 8080 has also been written for me."

That is, CP/M, the very system that was born on Intel's 8080, worked on the Z80 without any change. Zero moment. No rewriting. No hassle. No migration.

The business market turned toward the Z80 overnight. Not because anyone hated Intel. Not because the Z80 was magical. Just because they did not have to redo what they had already done.

And Kildall remained right there. Behind his desk. In front of the computer. With the eight-inch floppy.

But his shadow had fallen over everything.

---

The first person who understood was Roger Melen. A young engineer who, with his friend Harry Garland, had founded a company called Cromemco. Both were PhD students at Stanford. Both were in love with hardware.

The name Cromemco came from their shared dormitory at the university: Crothers Memorial. An old brick building reserved for engineering students.

They believed in the Z80 from the start. Before anyone had seen the chip, before the final price had been announced, they had placed their order. They had told Faggin: "However many you have, send them to us."

August 1976, one month after the Z80's official introduction. Cromemco introduced the first Z80-based computer: the Z-1. A twenty-two-slot chassis, the same famous IMSAI 8080 chassis. But its heart was no longer the 8080. Its heart was the Z80. Eight kilobytes of static RAM, one RS-232 serial port, one PROM programmer. Price: $2,495.

No contract. No promises. Just a chip sold, and a chip that worked. And Cromemco, without even placing a single line of advertising, found customers.

A year later, the Z-2 model came. With sixty-four kilobytes of RAM. With the ability to run CDOS, an operating system that imitated CP/M. With a price of $1,995. And most importantly: it was the first commercial computer that the US Navy certified without major modification. Some of these computers went aboard Ohio-class submarines. For recording test data.

A computer with a Z80 processor, in the heart of America's most advanced submarines.

This was a better slogan than any advertisement.

But Cromemco was not alone. NASA chose the Z80 to control laboratory equipment. The Chicago Mercantile Exchange bought a bank of sixty Cromemco Z-2 machines. For processing stock exchange transactions. Every day, millions of dollars passed through the Z80.

Radio Shack, the electronics store chain, sent the TRS-80 to market with the Z80. The first computer sold in ordinary stores. Anyone could go and pick up a box and bring it home.

Osborne, the newly founded company, put the Z80 into the world's first portable computer. A box the size of a suitcase, with a five-inch display. Sales went up.

Sinclair in England sent the ZX80 and ZX81 to market with the Z80. And then the ZX Spectrum. Millions of machines. It took all of Europe.

In Japan, NEC chose the Z80 as the central processor for the PC-8000 series. Sharp, Hitachi, Toshiba – all came, all took licenses, all started building Z80-based systems.

Within two years, the Z80's share of the 8-bit processor market passed the sixty percent mark. Intel and Motorola and MOS each had their own share. But the king was the Z80.

And not just in sales. In minds. A generation of engineers, programmers, inventors grew up with the Z80. For them the Z80 was not just a chip. It was their mother tongue. The first computer they took on a train, the first game they wrote, the first paycheck they earned with a computer – all passed through the Z80.

But this was not the end of the story.

In 1978, Intel introduced the 8086. The first 16-bit processor. Two years later, IBM used this same chip in its personal computer.

The world was moving toward 16-bit. Toward IBM. Toward a future in which the Z80 had grown old.

But the Z80 did not die. It went underground. Into the heart of ATMs. Into the heart of industrial controllers. Into the heart of fax machines. Into the heart of modems. Into the heart of Texas Instruments graphing calculators. Into the heart of millions of devices that no one saw, but all depended on the Z80.

sections.title: Section Two: Victory in the Business Sector — CP/M and the Software Empire
sections.content:
Monterey, California. The year 1973. Gary Kildall, a computer science professor at the Naval Postgraduate School, sat behind his desk. In front of him was a computer with an 8080 processor, and an eight-inch floppy drive that had just reached him stood out.

The problem was this: every computer maker had its own method for reading and writing to disk. A program that worked on one company's machine would not run at all on another company's machine. Kildall was tired of this chaos.

In the fall of 1974, in the back workshop of his house, Kildall began writing code. His friend John Torode was beside him that night. Colored wires hung from every side. Kildall transferred the program from paper tape to disk, then reset the system. The disk started spinning and the screen blinked.

Then a small prompt appeared on the screen: "*"

That symbol meant the disk was talking. It meant the processor and the drive and Kildall had finally found a common language. Kildall felt as though he had the power of an IBM supercomputer at his fingertips. All that power, gathered in a small box on his desk.

He named the program CP/M. A software layer that sat between the program and the hardware. It told the programmer: you just write your code, I will worry about the disk, the printer, and the memory.

Kildall's main innovation was this: he separated the hardware-dependent part and put it into a piece of code called BIOS. That is, for each new piece of hardware, only this piece had to be changed, and the rest of the system stayed in its place. Before CP/M, every computer company wrote its own operating system, and programs were not portable. CP/M broke this chain. A program that worked on one 8080 computer worked on any other computer with an 8080 or Z80, without changing even one line.

Kildall was still teaching at the university, but at night he sat behind the desk at home, copied the floppies, and put them in envelopes. The next morning he went to the post office. He sold the first CP/M license for ninety dollars. Then the next. And the next.

By 1977, CP/M had become the most popular microcomputer operating system in the world and ran on almost every computer that worked with the 8080 or Z80. A programmer could write his software once and be sure it would work on hundreds of different computer models. The software market became global from that point onward.

Now let us return to the Z80. The year 1976, the Z80 came to market with one simple promise: whatever has been written for the 8080 has also been written for me. That is, CP/M, the very system that was born on Intel's 8080, worked on the Z80 without any change. No rewriting, no migration, no hassle.

The business market turned toward the Z80 overnight. Not because anyone hated Intel, not because the Z80 was magical, just because they did not have to redo what they had already done. The software investment of companies had gone to a place where it was not loyal to the hardware, it was only loyal to CP/M. And the Z80 knew how to use this loyalty.

The first Z80-based business computers all worked with CP/M: the Cromemco Z-2 in 1977, NorthStar in the same year, and later the Osborne 1, Kaypro, and Vector Graphic. WordStar, the first professional word processor, dBASE II, the first popular database, and SuperCalc, the first spreadsheet for CP/M, all ran on the Z80, all thanks to CP/M.

A business computer in the late 1970s was not just a metal box; it was the processor, the memory, the disk controller, the input and output ports, the power supply, the chassis, the keyboard, the monitor, and most importantly, the operating system. The price of CP/M in those years for each machine was around one hundred to one hundred and fifty dollars. Alongside the seventy-dollar Z80 and the rest of the components, the final price of a business computer exceeded two thousand dollars. The Cromemco Z-2 in 1977 sold for about two thousand five hundred dollars. The ratio of the CPU price to the total system was around three to five percent.

That is, the business customer was not paying for the seventy-dollar Z80, nor even for the one hundred and fifty-dollar CP/M. He was paying for a two thousand five hundred-dollar machine that worked in his office, did typesetting, managed files, produced reports, and calculated employee salaries. This was exactly the point where the Z80 and CP/M carried each other. One built reliable hardware, the other built standard software. And neither took the other's place.

In 1978, companies like NEC, Sharp, and Toshiba licensed the Z80. In those same years, Digital Research also exported CP/M to Japan. No contract was signed between Zilog and Digital Research; there was no need. The market had naturally converged on a standard pair: Z80 and CP/M. And this pair ruled the world of business computers until the early 1980s.

Kildall, in the backyard of his house in Pacific Grove, that autumn night of 1974, perhaps did not know what fire he had lit. Perhaps he did know. Perhaps that was why he emptied the red wine with Torode and talked for hours. In that moment, there were only two men, one floppy drive, one blinking screen, and a prompt that changed the world: the small star that appeared on the screen.

The software written on the coast of California chained the hardware that ran across the world. And that chain, for a few years, belonged to the Z80.

But the East had no news of this. The East was still waiting.

sections.title: Section Three: Conquering the Homes — From Personal Computers to Game Consoles
sections.content:
Victory in the Second Arena

The Z80 had triumphed in the business market. Banks, offices, factories, and even US Navy submarines were using it. But there was another arena too: the homes. The place where fathers bought computers for their children. The place where teenagers played from dusk till dawn. The place where mothers were looking for an intelligent typewriter.

The price of CP/M and professional peripherals had kept the Z80 away from homes. A business computer with a Z80 and CP/M cost two thousand five hundred dollars. For an ordinary family, this meant six months' salary. No, another path was needed. A path that would bring the price under five hundred dollars.

And the Z80 needed no changes for this. It just needed new partners. Partners who would not sacrifice features for price.

Radio Shack: The Computer That Came from the Appliance Store

August 1977. Fort Worth, Texas. Radio Shack, the electronics store chain, introduced a computer named the TRS-80. Price: five hundred and ninety-five dollars. With a full keyboard, a monitor, and a simple cassette recorder for storing programs.

Dollar for dollar, it was the cheapest complete computer on the market. The Apple II came for six hundred and five dollars, but you had to buy the monitor and cassette recorder separately. The TRS-80 had everything. A ready-made box that went from the appliance store to the home.

The heart of this box was a Z80 with a frequency of 1.77 MHz. It had four kilobytes of RAM, but was expandable to forty-eight kilobytes. Its screen displayed sixty-four columns in sixteen rows of characters, and its graphics were only simple blocks. No, it was not for gaming. It was for work. It was for learning. It was for the home.

Radio Shack had its stores. Three thousand branches across America. A computer on the shelf of an appliance store, next to the radios and tape players. The customer came, saw, calculated the price, and took it home the same day.

In the first year, more than one hundred thousand machines were sold. In the industry, no one believed such a figure. Radio Shack had initially estimated it would sell three thousand. It sold one hundred thousand. The home market was thirsty. And the TRS-80 filled the first cup.

---

But Europe went its own way. And the man who built this path was Clive Sinclair.

Sinclair was not an ordinary man. In the Britain of the 1970s, he was known for his strange inventions: the pocket calculator, the pocket television, and later a three-wheeled electric car named the C5 that no one bought. But one thing was common in all his work: an obsession with miniaturization and cheapness. Sinclair believed technology should be as accessible as air. Not a luxury commodity for the wealthy.

His company, Sinclair Research, was based in Cambridge – a university city with a long tradition of mathematics and engineering. From the window of his office, the spires of King's College could be seen. But inside the office, there was no sign of the university's grandeur. Metal desks, graph paper, and engineers working on prototype boards until midnight.

When the Z80 came to market, Sinclair immediately saw its potential. This processor had all the integration that a cheap computer needed: an internal clock generator meant one less chip on the board. Internal Refresh meant yet one less chip. Single-voltage supply meant a simple and cheap power supply. For an engineer obsessed with reducing price, the Z80 was like a gift.

Sinclair gave his small team – led by a clever engineer named Jim Westwood – a simple order: "I want the price to be under one hundred pounds."

Reaching this price was pure madness. The cheapest computers of that time were at least three times this price. But Sinclair had a few tricks up his sleeve. First: a thin plastic case instead of metal. Second: a membrane keyboard instead of mechanical keys – a flat panel that worked with finger pressure, like a calculator. Third: selling as a kit. The customer soldered the parts himself. This both eliminated assembly costs and reduced taxes – in Britain, electronic kits had lower taxes.

The result was the ZX80. February 1980. Price: 79 pounds and 95 pence as a kit, 99 pounds and 95 pence assembled. A Z80 with a frequency of 3.25 MHz, one kilobyte of RAM, and a cassette recorder for storage. Its display was an ordinary television. Its body was so small it could be picked up with one hand – a white rectangle with a keyboard into which your finger sank and which had no tactile feedback.

The ZX80 was a marvel. Not because of processing power – which it lacked. Because of the price. Under one hundred pounds. Fathers could buy it for Christmas. Students could buy it with pocket money. Sales went up, higher than what Sinclair had imagined.

But the ZX80 also had problems. The membrane keyboard sometimes registered two letters at once. When a program was running, the screen went dark – because the Z80 switched between processing and displaying the image and its power was not enough for both. You had to stop the program to see what had happened. And worse: RAM was only one kilobyte. One kilobyte. Today a simple email has more volume than this.

In 1981, Sinclair released the ZX81. This time 69 pounds and 95 pence. RAM reached 2 kilobytes, expandable to 64 kilobytes with an add-on pack that attached to the back of the machine and constantly wobbled. The ZX81 sold more than one and a half million units. Sinclair was now a familiar name in every British home.

But he was not finished. In the small Cambridge laboratory, his team was working on something that would change everything. The ZX80 and ZX81 were black and white. In a world where American computers like the Apple II and Commodore 64 had color, this was a big weakness. Sinclair gave his team the mission to build a color computer, but not at the cost of losing their main advantage: cheapness.

The result was the ZX Spectrum. April 1982.

The name "Spectrum" came from its color capability. But Sinclair, as always, had found a cheap way to achieve color. Instead of a complex and expensive graphics chip, his engineers used a trick: they divided the display memory into two sections – one section for the pixel pattern with a resolution of 256 by 192, and a separate section for the colors. But the colors did not correspond to the pixels. Each 8 by 8 pixel block could only have two colors – one for the ink (foreground) and one for the paper (background). This limitation sometimes caused games to have "colour clash" – colors that seemed to spill out of the lines, like a child's painting that had gone outside the lines. But game developers turned this very limitation into a unique visual style that is still instantly recognizable today.

The ZX Spectrum was offered in two models: 16 kilobytes of RAM at 125 pounds, and 48 kilobytes at 175 pounds. A Z80A processor with a frequency of 3.5 MHz. Fifteen colors, including black and white, with the ability to display two brightness levels for each color – meaning colors could be "bright" or "dark." Sound output was through a small beeper – not an advanced sound chip like the Commodore 64's SID, just a tiny speaker that could beep and click. Nevertheless, creative programmers later produced multi-part music from this very beeper that is still worth listening to.

Programs were saved on cassette tape. Tapes whose loading sometimes took five minutes. The screen during this time showed flashing colored stripes – horizontal blue and yellow for the pilot signal, horizontal red and cyan for data. And then, sometimes in the fourth minute, the famous message appeared: R Tape loading error. You would take the tape out, adjust it a little, put it back in. From the beginning.

But it was the Spectrum's design that made it iconic. A small black case, the size of a paperback book. A rubber keyboard with keys that resembled erasers. Forty keys, but each had up to six functions. To type the word PRINT, you pressed the P key. For LOAD, you pressed the J key. Each key typed a complete BASIC word – an input system that became known as "touch-typing vocabulary." Newcomers were confused: why was Z both P and the quotation mark? But professionals coded on these keyboards with unbelievable speed. Their fingers memorized which key gave which command.

Programming with the Spectrum was easy. You turned it on, and in less than two seconds you entered directly into the Sinclair BASIC interpreter. No disk, no operating system to boot, no error message. Just a blinking cursor on a black screen. You typed and it ran. For millions of British children, this was their first programming experience. They started by typing in codes printed in magazines – full pages of BASIC commands that took hours to enter. And then, they started changing them. Gradually they learned. And some of them became the game development giants of tomorrow.

And then, the games came.

Between 1983 and 1987, thousands of games were written for the Spectrum – from the bedrooms of teenagers who coded after school, from small companies formed in garages, from programmers who went on Saturday mornings by bicycle to the publisher's office to deliver the cassette of their new game.

Some of these games are legendary today:

Manic Miner (1983): created by sixteen-year-old Matthew Smith. A miner with a yellow hat who traversed twenty caverns collecting keys. Robots, spiders, and giant penguins pursued him. Twenty precisely designed screens, each a separate puzzle. Smith wrote this game in eight weeks – one teenager, one Spectrum, and eight weeks. The game became so popular that stores ran out of stock.

Jet Set Willy (1984): the sequel to Manic Miner. This time the miner was trapped in a large house with sixty rooms – after a party that had lasted until dawn, he had to clean the house. The game was so big it had a famous bug: it could not be completed. Some items were in rooms that, when entered, would corrupt the game. Smith later confessed that he had sent the game to the publisher without full testing – the deadline was near.

Elite (1985): created by two Cambridge students named David Braben and Ian Bell. A 3D space game with vector graphics. In a galaxy with eight galaxies and over two thousand planets. The player could be a trader, a space pirate, or a bounty hunter. No one had ever seen such scale on a 48-kilobyte computer. The game was open – you went wherever you wanted, did whatever you wanted. A concept that years later reached its peak in Grand Theft Auto.

The Great Escape (1986): based on the film The Great Escape. A prisoner of war in a German camp who had to escape. The guards had a daily routine – food, exercise, roll call. The player had to learn the routine and use the gaps. The game's artificial intelligence was a masterpiece for its time.

And hundreds of other titles: Chuckie Egg in which a poultry farmer climbed ladders and collected eggs. Sabre Wulf with cartoon graphics and a jungle maze. Skool Daze in which a schoolboy had to escape from teachers and steal his report card. Head Over Heels with isometric graphics and two characters who had to cooperate to solve puzzles. Names that for a generation are like poetry.

The British game industry was born on the Spectrum. Companies like Ocean Software, Ultimate Play The Game, and Melbourne House started from nothing and became multi-million-pound giants. In a village in Liverpool, the Darling brothers – David and Richard – started a company called Bug-Byte and later built Codemasters, which today is one of the world's largest game publishers.

By 1985, five million Spectrum machines had been sold. In Britain, one in every three homes had a Spectrum. And each of these homes had a story: the night the cassette tape loaded for five minutes and then gave an R Tape loading error. The night the game finally loaded and they stayed awake until dawn. The brother who knew how to code and the sister who only played games. The father who had bought the Spectrum for "work" and secretly played Jet Set Willy at night. The mother who saved the shopping list in memory and proudly showed it to her friends.

But Sinclair was restless. In 1984, he released the QL – a 16-bit computer with a Motorola 68008 processor. It was supposed to be the Spectrum's successor. But it failed – its case had problems, its microdrives were unreliable, and its price was high. In 1986, Sinclair Research, on the verge of bankruptcy, was sold to Amstrad. Alan Sugar, the head of Amstrad, bought the rights to all Sinclair products – including the Spectrum.

Amstrad made three more models: the Spectrum +2 with a built-in cassette recorder, the Spectrum +3 with a 3-inch floppy drive, and the Spectrum +2A with a redesigned case. These models still sold, but the world was changing. 16-bit computers were taking the market. By 1992, production of the Spectrum was stopped. Ten years after its birth.

But the spirit of the Spectrum did not die. In Russia and Eastern Europe, Spectrum clones were being built until the late 1990s – because they were cheap and their parts were available. Thousands of its games were etched into the minds of a generation who later became programmers, game designers, musicians, and engineers. And to this day, internet forums, modern remakes, and even new games are published for the Spectrum.

sections.title: Section Four: The Z80 Enters the Playing Field
sections.content:
But the Z80 was not only in the office and the home. It was also in the arcades. The year 1980, the company Namco in Japan made a game called Pac-Man. A yellow circle that ran through a maze eating dots. Four ghosts chased him. It seemed simple, but it created such an addiction that to this day, it is the most iconic game in history.

The heart of Pac-Man was a Z80. One. Just that.

The year 1981, the company Sega made the game Scramble. This time two Z80s worked inside the machine. One for game logic, one for sound and graphics. The year 1982, Galaga came with three Z80s. The golden age of arcade games was the age of the Z80.

And then, home consoles. The year 1982, ColecoVision. The year 1986, the Sega Master System. The year 1990, the Sega Game Gear. All with the Z80. And the year 1991, the Nintendo Game Boy. Its processor was not a Z80. It was a copy of the Z80. Made by Sharp. Its name was LR35902. But its heart was the same. The same architecture. The same eight bits. The same 158 instructions. Just one small difference: you could not run original Z80 code on it. But it was a close cousin. First-degree family.

---

Now the Z80 had conquered the homes of the West. From American submarines to cheap computers. From ATMs to school calculators. From arcades to the pockets of millions of children with the Game Boy.

But another world, on the other side of the Pacific Ocean, in the land of the rising sun, was waiting. Not for war, but for commerce. And not for theft, but for partnership.

Japan was waiting. With factories ready, engineers hungry, and checks placed on the table, without even speaking a word.

It was the turn of the allies.

sections.title: Section One: Continental Europe — Beyond the English Channel
sections.content:
In the previous chapter we saw how the Z80 conquered Britain — through the ZX Spectrum and the Amstrad CPC and thousands of young programmers who made games in their bedrooms. But Britain was only a part of Europe. On the other side of the English Channel, in France, West Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, and Spain, the Z80 was traveling a different path — not through a single best-selling computer like the Spectrum, but through dozens of different models, each taking a share of the market, and each having its own story.

France, unlike Britain, did not surrender to Sinclair's temptation. The French wanted their own computer — made in France, for France. The French government in the early 1980s launched a national program for the development of home computers: the "Informatique pour tous" plan. The result was the Thomson family.

The Thomson MO5 entered the market in 1984 at a competitive price. A Z80 processor, sixteen kilobytes of RAM, and a light pen instead of a mouse — because the French believed a light pen was better than a mouse for design and education. The MO5 became the standard computer in French schools. Thousands of French students learned programming with the MO5. The TO7, which had come a year earlier, with better graphics and software cartridges, had targeted the home market. Its colors were livelier, its sound was better, and most importantly, French games ran on it — games that were in their mother tongue, with characters from French culture.

At the same time, the company Matra-Hachette entered the field with the Alice 90. The Alice 90 was essentially a copy of the American TRS-80, but with French design, an AZERTY keyboard instead of QWERTY, and an operating system inspired by CP/M. Although the Alice 90 could not compete with Thomson — Thomson's sales were several times higher — it further established the Z80 name in France. The French now had a choice: Thomson for education and games, Alice for more serious work.

West Germany, however, went its own way. There, the computer was not just a work tool; it was a serious hobby, a branch of engineering that had to be built with obsessive German precision. The Germans loved precise engineering, and the Z80, with its powerful and clean architecture, captured their hearts.

The Schneider CPC — the German version of the Amstrad CPC we saw in the previous chapter — became intensely popular in Germany. Schneider, the German company that had previously made audio equipment, licensed the production of the CPC from Amstrad and sent it to market with German standards. A keyboard with spring-loaded keys, a hundred-page manual in German, and a two-year warranty — things that were unheard of in Britain and France. The CPC in Germany was not just a computer; it was an investment. Germans wrote software for it, printed books, and even published a dedicated magazine for it.

Before Schneider, the company Grundig — the same German radio and television giant — had also entered the game. Grundig used the Z80 in its various models, including professional word processing systems used in German offices. Triumph-Adler also entered with the AlphaTronic — a business computer with a Z80 and CP/M designed for accounting and warehouse management. The Germans wanted the Z80 not just in the home, but in the office and the factory too.

In the Netherlands, Philips — the European electronics giant that made everything from light bulbs to medical equipment — sent the P2000 family to market with the Z80. The P2000M was a business computer with two floppy drives and the ability to run CP/M. The P2000T was the home model with a strange design: a white box with a built-in television and cartridges that resembled video tapes. Philips later also cooperated with the MSX standard and took the Z80 into Dutch and Belgian homes in various models like the VG-8020 and VG-8235.

Italy did not sit idle either. The company Olivetti — the same typewriter giant whose machines once filled every office in Europe — entered the computer age with the M20. The M20 used the Z8000 (Zilog's 16-bit processor), but its input/output section worked with a Z80. Olivetti later also built smaller personal computers with the Z80 that sold in the Italian and Spanish markets.

Spain, with companies like Amstrad España (the Spanish branch of Amstrad) and Investrónica, which built Spectrum-compatible computers, created a passionate market for the Z80. The Inves Spectrum+ was a legal copy of the Spectrum with a better keyboard and improved video output that found many fans in Spain and Portugal.

Continental Europe, unlike Britain, never had a single "national computer." France had Thomson, Germany had Schneider and Grundig, the Netherlands had Philips, Italy had Olivetti. Each country built its own computer, with its own standards, for its own market. But one thing was common in all of them: their beating heart was the Z80. From Amsterdam to Madrid, from Paris to Munich, the Z80 was silently conquering all of Europe.

And then, it was the turn of the standard that gathered everyone under one roof: MSX. But this standard was built not by the Europeans, but by the Japanese. And the story of MSX is the story of Japan.

sections.title: Section Two: Japan — A Partner in the East
sections.content:
The Z80 had triumphed in America and Europe. But Japan, its case was different.

Japan in the 1970s was not a country that imitated the West. It was a country that built better than the West. Automobiles, cameras, audio equipment — whatever the Americans designed, the Japanese sent a better version to market with a lower price and higher quality. The semiconductor industry was no exception to this rule. NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, Sharp, Fujitsu — each had built modern factories, trained hundreds of engineers, and were thirsty for new technical knowledge.

When the Z80 was introduced in July 1976, the Japanese were the first to knock on Zilog's door.

In that very first week, a man in a dark suit entered Zilog's office in Los Altos. He placed four one-hundred-dollar bills on the table and said: "Two chips." Ungermann asked which company he was from; the man did not answer, took the chips, and left. A few hours later, another man came — the same behavior, the same silence. Faggin looked at Ungermann and said: "The copying began before the selling."

But NEC did not just want to copy. It wanted to be a partner.

The Z80 license agreement with NEC was signed in that same year, 1976 — one of Zilog's first and most important contracts. NEC obtained the right to manufacture the Z80 and sent its chips to market under the name μPD780C. The technical specifications were the same, only the name was different. This "second source" strategy was common in the semiconductor industry in those years: a single chip could be bought from several different companies — Zilog, NEC, Sharp, Toshiba. Each made the Z80, each under its own name. But the market only knew the Z80.

That same year, NEC sent an educational kit named the TK-80 to market: a small board with a μPD780C processor, a few keys, and a few LED displays. It was meant for engineers to learn how a computer worked. But something happened that no one predicted: the TK-80 became a cultural phenomenon among Japanese engineers and students. They turned this simple board into a small computer — they wrote programs, made games, taught each other. The TK-80 was no longer an educational kit; it was a spark. Millions of people became acquainted with the Z80 for the first time, without knowing its name.

In 1979, NEC introduced its first real computer: the PC-8001. A Z80 processor with a frequency of 4 MHz, 64 kilobytes of RAM, and the ability to display Kanji characters — something no American computer could do. It was for the professional market — offices, companies. The Japanese bought from the Japanese, and NEC, with the Z80, told them: "We can do it too. Even better." By 1981, the PC-8001 held forty percent of Japan's personal computer market. IBM had not yet entered, Apple had not penetrated, Commodore was not there at all.

In November 1981, NEC went further with the PC-8801. The same Z80, but this time with eight-color graphics, sound, a disk port, and upgrade capability. The PC-8801 was for everything — office, home, games. The company Enix, which later gained worldwide fame with "Dragon Quest," wrote its games first for the PC-8801. The company Koei, with its historical strategy games, did the same. The PC-8801 became the heart of Japan's game industry. By November 1983, more than 170,000 units had been sold — just in Japan. A market the Americans could not enter, because they did not know its language. But the Z80 did.

The PC-8800 remained so popular that it was still being produced until the early 1990s. In the world of computers, ten years means several generations. But the PC-8800 stayed, because the Japanese had grown up with it. And when you grow up with something, you do not let it go.

But NEC was only one of the players. Sharp, its long-time rival, had entered the computer market long before with the MZ series. The MZ-80K, introduced in 1978, was one of Japan's first personal computers — a big box with a built-in keyboard and a separate monitor, with a Z80 at its heart. Unlike the PC-8001, which was for offices, the MZ-80K went more to homes and enthusiasts. Sharp later built the MZ-700 and MZ-800 — computers that could work both with Sharp's own software and with CP/M.

Sony also entered the field. The company we know today for the PlayStation entered the computer world in the 1980s with the SMC-70 and SMC-777. The SMC-70 was a professional computer with a Z80A, 3.5-inch floppy drives, and the ability to run CP/M. Sony built this computer for the engineering and industrial design market, with advanced graphics capabilities that were rare at the time. The SMC-777, which came in 1982, was a cheaper, more home-oriented version.

Casio, a company more famous for calculators and watches, entered with the FP-1100 — a compact computer with a Z80 designed mostly for educational and home use. The FP-1100 may not have been as successful as NEC and Sharp, but it showed that the Z80 was penetrating all layers of the Japanese market.

And then, one of the strangest computers ever built with the Z80: the Yamaha CX5M.

Everyone knew Yamaha for motorcycles and pianos. But in 1984, this company built a computer that was specifically for music. The CX5M was a complete MSX-based computer with a Z80 at its heart, but it had one fundamental difference: a built-in FM synthesizer with the Yamaha YM2151 sound chip. Professional musicians could make music with the CX5M, write notes, and simulate the sound of different instruments. The CX5M was the first computer that targeted musicians, not programmers. In Japanese recording studios, the CX5M could be found. And all of this ran on a single Z80.

But the biggest event in the Japanese computer world happened in 1983. Kazuhiko Nishi — the head of ASCII Corporation and a close friend of Bill Gates — had an ambitious idea: a global standard for home computers, like VHS for video. They named it MSX.

The MSX specification was like a recipe: a Zilog Z80 processor with a frequency of 3.58 MHz, Texas Instruments TMS9918 graphics with sixteen colors, sound via the AY-3-8910 chip with three channels, and the MSX BASIC and MSX-DOS operating systems, which were inspired by CP/M. Any company could build an MSX — Sony, Panasonic, Casio, Sanyo, Toshiba, Hitachi, Fujitsu, Sharp, Mitsubishi, and dozens of other companies. All with the Z80, all with the same software, all compatible with each other.

The first MSX came to market in October 1983: the Mitsubishi ML-8000. After that, the floodgates opened. By 1985, millions of MSX machines had been sold in Japan — estimates vary from 3 to 9 million. The statistical discrepancy itself shows how explosive the sales were. The MSX in Japan was a success beyond expectation. In Europe it had moderate sales (Philips was the largest producer of MSX in Europe), in America almost none — because Commodore and Apple had seized the market. But Japan was completely under the rule of the MSX, and in the heart of every MSX beat a Z80.

But the Z80 was not only in computers. Japan in the 1980s was the world's largest producer of fax machines, and many of these machines — from the brands Canon, Ricoh, Panasonic, and Brother — worked with a Z80. In fax machines, the Z80 was responsible for image compression, memory management, and keyboard control. Millions of fax machines around the world, without anyone knowing, had a Z80 in their hearts.

But the most ambitious move was made by Hitachi. In 1985, Hitachi introduced the HD64180: a supercharged Z80. This chip was not just a copy; it was a complete redesign with an advanced Memory Management Unit (MMU) that allowed addressing up to one megabyte — sixteen times more than the original Z80. Two DMA channels for fast data transfer, two serial ports, and an internal timer. And all of this while maintaining full compatibility with the Z80. Hitachi licensed this chip to Zilog, and Zilog later sent it to market under the name Z180 — a chip that itself opened a new chapter in the life of the Z80 and was used in industrial controllers and embedded systems for decades to come.

The Japanese companies had taken Zilog seriously — not as a rival, but as a partner. A partner who sold its knowledge, and the Japanese used that knowledge to build an empire. By the early 1980s, NEC held more than fifty percent of Japan's personal computer market. And most of these computers worked with the Z80.

sections.title: Section Three: Latin America — The Republic of Copied Computers
sections.content:
In the south of the American continent, in countries whose economies were just beginning to breathe, the computer was still a luxury commodity. An IBM or Apple machine cost several times the average annual salary of a worker. Imports were restricted, tariffs were high, and unofficial sanctions had closed the paths. But there was a thirst — a thirst for technology, for learning, for the future that the West had and the South was deprived of.

And the Z80, as always, opened its own way.

Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, had enacted strict laws on computer imports in the early 1980s. The government wanted domestic industry to grow. IBM and Apple could not easily enter. But Brazilian engineers did not sit idle. They decided to build computers themselves — with available parts, with knowledge they learned from foreign magazines, and most importantly, with the Z80.

The first spark was struck by the company Prológica. In October 1981, they introduced the NE-Z80: a complete copy of the Sinclair ZX80. The same Z80A with a frequency of 3.25 MHz, the same one kilobyte of RAM, the same membrane keyboard. Price: 59,900 cruzeiros — six times the minimum monthly wage, but still half the price of an original imported machine.

The NE-Z80 succeeded and Prológica built later models too: the CP-200 (a copy of the ZX81 with 16 kilobytes of RAM), and then the TK90X and TK95 — copies of the ZX Spectrum that gained strange popularity in Brazil. Their rival Microdigital did not stop either: the TK82 (a copy of the ZX80), the TK83 (expandable to 64 kilobytes of RAM), and the TK85, whose appearance resembled the Spectrum but whose insides were the same old ZX81 with 10 kilobytes of RAM.

The Brazilians did not just copy; sometimes they also innovated. The TK90X, which came in 1985, was a direct copy of the Spectrum with a modified video circuit for a clearer picture, error messages in Portuguese, and two new BASIC commands: TRACE and UDG. These changes sometimes created incompatibility — some Spectrum games would not run on it — but the Brazilians had enough local software, written by themselves for themselves.

Copying computers in Brazil became an industry. Prológica and Microdigital were only two names among dozens of companies that built Z80-based computers.
