They even copied the peripherals: printers, disk drives, and even mice. But this industry was short-lived. In the late 1980s, MSX computers entered Brazil — cheaper, more powerful, and original. The market for copied computers folded one by one. Prológica shut down, Microdigital too. But their legacy remained: a generation of engineers and programmers who grew up with the Z80 and later built Brazil's software industry.

Argentina went down a similar path, with one difference: instead of Sinclair, they went after Timex.

The company Czerweny Electronica, which previously made ceiling fan motors, entered the computer industry out of necessity — the market for ceiling motors was shrinking, computers were growing. In 1983, they introduced the CZ-1500: a copy of the Timex Sinclair 1500, with a Z80A and 16 kilobytes of RAM. But it had one vital advantage: video output with the PAL-N standard specific to Argentina. Imported computers usually worked with PAL-B and their picture on Argentine televisions came out black-and-white or blurry. The CZ-1500 had a clear and colorful picture — even on old televisions. This small advantage guaranteed sales.

Then came the CZ-2000: a complete copy of the ZX Spectrum with 48 kilobytes of RAM and 16 kilobytes of ROM. Price: 310 dollars — more expensive than the Brazilian TK90X, but with higher quality. Czerweny imported the motherboard from the company Sinclair in Portugal and assembled it in Argentina. The result was a machine with full compatibility with the original Spectrum. Imported games ran without problem.

Czerweny built several more models: the CZ Spectrum, with two joystick ports. The CZ Spectrum Plus, in a new case with a better keyboard. But the Argentine market was small — its population a fifth of Brazil's, and its economy sicker. Rampant inflation doubled the price of computers every month. Yet, for those who could afford it, the CZ-2000 was a dream.

Czerweny was not alone. The company Drean, which previously made washing machines, competed with the Commodore 64. Tonomac entered with various Z80 models. But none were as successful as Czerweny. Czerweny continued production until the late 1980s. Then, like many others, it surrendered to MSX and Japanese computers and returned to its previous work: ceiling fan motors.

Mexico, however, went a different path. It neither copied nor imported — it designed.

Between 1979 and 1982, the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) carried out a project named AHR: a parallel processing computer with sixty-four Z80 processors arranged in a ring. A hardware distributor divided tasks among them. Memory was split into active and inactive sections. The entire system was designed to run only one programming language: Lisp.

The AHR prototype was completed in late 1982 — an engineering masterpiece. But nothing more. No one used it, no software was written for it, and no company agreed to produce it. The AHR remained just a research project — but it was the first computer entirely designed in Mexico.

In those same years, the Autonomous University of Puebla (BUAP) built the SMU system: a motherboard with an S-100 bus to which up to 64 terminals could connect. The heart of the system was a Z80, the operating system a modified version of CP/M for multi-user capability. Students learned programming simultaneously without each having a separate computer. By 1983, 64 terminals were connected to the SMU.

And then, the Turing-850 project. It began in mid-1981. The goal: to design a computer that could easily be produced in Mexico. The innovation: two Z80 processors — one as master for the operating system and application programs, the other as slave for input/output and graphics. A Z80A with a frequency of 6 MHz was responsible for the main calculations, a Z80B at 4 MHz was responsible for graphics and the keyboard. Division of labor like big computers, price like small computers.

The prototype was completed in late 1984. It was supposed to be transferred to Mexican industry. But no company stepped forward. The project remained without a customer and, like AHR and SMU, was consigned to oblivion.

Uruguay, Chile, Venezuela, Colombia — each had its own story with the Z80. In Uruguay, Spectrum and MSX computers were imported from Argentina and Brazil. In Chile, the market was small but thirsty. In Venezuela, despite oil revenues, imports were restricted and the Z80 entered through the gray market.

And Cuba — an island under the strictest American sanctions — also found the Z80. Through Eastern Bloc countries, through intermediaries, through parts smuggled in travelers' suitcases. Cuba built its own computers with the Z80, including models for education that were used in schools. Sanctions could not stop the Z80. The Z80 crossed even the wall of sanctions.

Latin America never knew the Z80 as widely as North America or Europe — not because of the Z80's weakness, but because of the weakness of the economy. People had no money, the market was small, the industry was fledgling. But the Z80 was the only processor that found its way into this deprived continent. In Brazil, a generation grew up with the TK90X. In Argentina, with the CZ-2000. In Mexico, with the SMU and Turing-850. And these same engineers, years later, built Latin America's software industry — banking systems, accounting software, video games. Everything started with the Z80.

sections.title: Section Four: Across the Oceans
sections.content:
In Canada, the market was too small to form an independent story, but the Spectrum and Amstrad CPC had acceptable sales. Commodore had a production line in Ontario, but worked mostly with the 6502. The Z80 in Canada came mostly through imports from America and Britain.

In Australia, the company Dick Smith Electronics built the VZ-200 and VZ-300 computers with the Z80A — sales not in the millions, but significant for Australia's small population market. In New Zealand, Sinclair and Amstrad computers were the cheapest option.

---

The Z80 had now become global. From American submarines to Tokyo arcades, from Paris classrooms to São Paulo workshops, from Osaka music studios to Mexico City laboratories. Few chips in history have reached this geographical breadth.

But one part of the world still remained. A place where the Z80 entered not through commercial contracts, but through reverse engineering and secret copies. A place where the Z80 was not just a chip — it was a weapon in the Cold War.

The Eastern Bloc was waiting. And the story of the Z80 on the other side of the Iron Curtain is perhaps the strangest chapter in the life of this chip.

sections.title: Section One: The Siege and the Hunt
sections.content:
The Z80 had traveled from ocean to ocean in the West. From the submarines of the US Navy to the home computers of Britain, from the factories of Japan to the graphing calculators of Brazil. Wherever there was a computer, somewhere a Z80 was breathing.

But half the world sat in darkness.

The Iron Curtain had split Europe in two. East and West were separated not only politically and militarily, but technologically as well. In the West, computers rolled off production lines. In the East, engineers read Western blueprints with magnifying glasses, trying to understand what "computer" meant.

The Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls – CoCom – was established in 1949 by Western countries. Its members were all NATO members (except Iceland), along with Japan and Australia. Their goal was this: "the technological siege of the Eastern Bloc."

This prohibition covered many products: powerful computers, telecommunications equipment, industrial machinery, advanced software, and most importantly, microelectronics. Anything that could help Soviet military or industrial advancement remained behind this wall of prohibition.

A secret CIA report described the bitter reality thus: "Western export license restrictions curb the sale of computers from West to East. Often, the very sales that are forbidden are those the Soviet Union is most eager for."

That is, the thirstier the East became, the tighter the West shut the door. This was a vicious circle. A complete siege.

But let us be honest. The sanctions were like a coin with two faces.

The first face: the technological backwardness of the East. The Eastern Bloc was deprived of legal access to Western technology. They were forced to obtain every component either through intermediaries, through reverse engineering, or through espionage. And this process was always slower, more expensive, and of lower quality than the original. Available records show that the value of exception requests for importing technology into the Eastern Bloc, between 1967 and 1970, exceeded 40 million dollars.

The second face: the starving of the East. The harsher the sanctions became, the greater the appetite for Western technology grew. And hunger drives a person to any door. There was no choice but another way: industrial espionage, technology theft, and large-scale copying.

Estimates indicate that the process of reverse engineering and copying Western technology in the Eastern Bloc, in the computer sector alone, brought more than one billion dollars in savings. A number that, in those years, was dazzling.

The Eastern Bloc countries, deprived of legal access to Western technology, each tried in some way to bridge this gap. Czechoslovakia and Hungary had each submitted 9 exception requests for technology imports to CoCom, Poland 7 requests. These countries were the hungriest in the Eastern Bloc. And each chose a technological hero. Poland and Czechoslovakia and Hungary went after Intel's 8080 architecture. Bulgaria copied the Motorola 6800 and the Commodore 6502. East Germany, however, made a different decision.

East Germany chose the Z80.

Not because it was the best. Because it reached the front line sooner than the rest. Because the Stasi (East Germany's secret police) understood sooner than the rest that this chip was the master key to the future. And because German engineers had the audacity to choose the hardest path: copying the most advanced chip on the market.

In 1976, the Z80 came to market. In 1977, only one year later, East Germany shifted its industrial espionage focus from Intel to Zilog. This means the speed of the Stasi's operations rivaled the speed of Western technological developments.

This was the moment when history took a different path.

sections.title: Section Two: The Stasi and Operation Shadow
sections.content:
In East Germany, no one was sitting idle.

The German Democratic Republic, the most advanced country in the Eastern Bloc, was under the Stasi's magnifying glass. But the Stasi was not only for repression. The Stasi was also for theft. Technology theft. Theft of the future.

The Fourteenth Department of the Stasi's Main Directorate for Foreign Intelligence was a secret unit whose task was defined as industrial espionage in the information technology industry. Code name: Abteilung XIV. Their job: finding the blueprints of Western microprocessors, stealing them, and delivering them to German engineers.

This department worked closely with the company Carl Zeiss Jena, a company specialized in optics, computers, and laser research. The Stasi itself called this company the "child of the Main Directorate for Foreign Intelligence." A "branch office" of the Fourteenth Department was stationed right inside the Zeiss Jena factory to deliver information and materials directly to the company. No filter. No intermediary. Just the chip, from Silicon Valley to the East German production line.

The Stasi relied for this operation on a vast network of spies in the West. The geographical proximity of East Germany to West Germany, and the initially open borders, had allowed them from the earliest years to place their infiltrators in the heart of European industry. After the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961, the method changed. There were no more spies crossing the border. Now it was the turn of recruitment. Recruiting engineers, recruiting scientists, recruiting anyone with access to technology.

Most of the spies working for the Stasi in the West were employed men. Engineers. Science graduates. Some worked in personnel departments, others were businessmen. They were not necessarily senior managers or department heads. Sometimes a mid-level engineer, like Dieter Feuerstein (code name "Petermann") at the company MBB, was enough to steal top-secret military blueprints. Or Peter Alwart (code name "Alfred") at AEG/Telefunken, who worked as an engineer. Or Peter Kohler (code name "Schulze"), who worked for Texas Instruments.

In 1971, with Erich Honecker's rise to power, scientific-technical espionage in the Eastern Bloc increased sharply. The Stasi's state security unit expanded its work to counter the technological sanctions. By the end of the eighties, the Stasi's scientific-technical espionage department had around five hundred employees. Of these, nearly two hundred were directly active in espionage operations. They had nineteen members who held doctoral degrees.

A Stasi agent later revealed what capital lay behind these operations. He estimated that the development cost of the MVS operating system for IBM was around two billion dollars. But East Germany spent only two hundred million East German marks to copy the same system and transfer it to their own hardware. Fifty-seven million dollars, against two billion. A ratio of one to thirty-five.

"From this, the vast economic advantage brought by the operational activity of the science and technology section is completely apparent" — this is what the Stasi agents had written in their secret reports.

Why Silicon Valley? Why was the Stasi able to infiltrate the heart of the Western technology industry so easily?

The answer is simple: Silicon Valley, in those years, was a small village. Engineers moved from one company to another without even changing their homes. Competitors were on the same neighboring street. Industrial secrets were whispered behind the thin walls of offices.

As a secret document later revealed: "For the Stasi, these conditions were ideal, because the area where America's leading microelectronics specialists were stationed was very manageable. To change jobs, they did not even have to move. For implementing long-term operational measures, these conditions were ideal."

The year 1976, the Z80 came to market. The year 1977, only one year later, the Stasi's focus shifted. The first microprocessor information reached the Stasi in 1975. Sixteen pieces of intelligence, all but one about Intel. But two years later, the focus shifted from Intel to Zilog.

They stole the technical documents and blueprints of the Z80 from Silicon Valley. How? This secret has still not been revealed. Former Stasi agents had sworn not to disclose the details of the operation. But the result was clear: East Germany had reached the Z80. Without a license. Without money. Only with effort and audacity.

In a secret report, Stasi agents wrote: "We obtained the blueprints and technology of the INTEL 8080 and ZILOG Z80 microprocessors from Silicon Valley in California."

Carl Zeiss Jena, the largest optics company in East Germany, had a Stasi branch office inside it. Information went directly from the front line of espionage to the production line. Without filter. Without delay. On November 27, 1986, Professor Doctor Wolfgang Biermann, the head of Carl Zeiss Jena, submitted a formal request: "Documents and samples of the 1-megabit chip." Request number: 51,87,00086. 51 for Carl Zeiss Jena, 87 the year of the request, and 86 the serial number. A year later, on September 3, 1988, a source code-named "Joker" run by the Stasi's Fifteenth Department obtained the 1-megabit chip technology.

By 1989, these efforts had increased East Germany's productivity in the information technology sector by 39.2 percent. Despite this, East Germany was still behind West Germany. But the gap was no longer the gap.

In 1976, the Ninth Congress of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany set a new political goal: "Accelerating the introduction of the achievements of scientific and technological progress into the production of consumer goods." At the head of this goal was "a significant increase in products in the mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and electronics sectors." And most importantly: "the standardization of parts and sections."

East Germany wanted to have its own standard. A standard not dependent on the West. A standard it set itself. And for this, it needed the Z80.

sections.title: Section Three: Born in the East — The U880 and Its Children
sections.content:
The result of this operation reached the production line in 1980. The U880, an exact copy of the Z80, was born at the VEB Mikroelektronik "Karl Marx" in Erfurt. The same number of pins. The same frequency. The same power.

This chip was nothing but a copy of the Z80. But not a simple copy. The German engineers not only copied the chip, but also built a complete family of peripheral chips: the U855D copy of the Z80 PIO, the U8560D copy of the Z80 SIO, the U857D copy of the Z80 CTC, the UA858D copy of the Z80 DMA, the U8272D copy of the Intel 8272 floppy disk controller. A complete ecosystem. It was as if Zilog, under another name, had been born in the heart of East Germany. German engineers could build any system that worked with the Z80 using their own components. Without dependence on the West. Without the need for smuggling.

The U880 was produced in several different versions: the U880D standard version with a frequency of 2.5 MHz for general use, the UA880D high-speed version with a frequency of 4 MHz, the UB880D improved version with a wider temperature range, the VB880D industrial and military version with a temperature range of -25 to +85 degrees Celsius, and the UD880D weakened version with a frequency of 1 MHz for entertainment and education. Each of these versions had its own specific job. The VB880Ds went into military equipment. The UA880Ds went into office computers. The UD880Ds went into the hands of schoolchildren.

But the U880 was not a perfect copy. The German engineers, perhaps because of Faggin's traps, perhaps because of technological limitations, could not copy everything exactly. Some instructions, those that were harder to copy, had been omitted. One small difference: in the OUTI instruction, when the counter reached zero, the CY flag was not set. A subtle difference. No one would notice. Except a professional programmer who had stared at his code for hours. But these differences did not matter. The U880 worked. And that was everything.

On every U880, a date code was engraved. Two letters. The first for the year, the second for the month. F for 1975, H for 1976, I for 1977, K for 1978, L for 1979, M for 1980. And then, N for 1981, P for 1982, R for 1983, S for 1984, T for 1985, U for 1986, V for 1987, W for 1988, X for 1989, A for 1990, B for 1991. The month with one digit: 1 to 9 for January to September, 0 for October, N for November, D for December.

A simple code. But it told the history of an empire. An empire that, from 1980 to 1991, produced millions of chips annually. And then, the Wall fell. And the empire, like many other things, disappeared.

In the Soviet Union, they went a different path. They decided to use Intel's 8080 instead of the Z80. Not because the 8080 was better, but because they had more information about it. Soviet espionage had focused on Intel for years. The result: the KR580VM80A. A chip that reached mass production in 1979. Five years after the original 8080. With a frequency of 2 to 2.5 MHz. With 6-micrometer technology.

A Soviet engineer later revealed: "The KR580VM80A was not a pure copy; it was more a product of reverse engineering. After analyzing the original, they corrected some flaws in the original circuit. It can be called an improved version of the 8080." The Soviets did not just copy; sometimes they also made better.

But the KR580VM80A had one flaw. There was a bug in the interrupt logic. If a CALL instruction came during the INTA cycle and the INT input remained active, the chip would not clear the internal interrupt flag. The result: an infinite loop. The chip would keep acknowledging the interrupt and pushing the program counter onto the stack until the stack overflowed. Fortunately, in most circuits, the 8259A interrupt controller hid this problem. But the bug existed. And no one could do anything.

The KR580 family was complete. It was not just the processor. The Soviets copied a complete family of peripheral chips: the KR580VV51A copy of the Intel 8251, the KR580VI53 copy of the 8253 timer, the KR580VV55A copy of the 8255 parallel interface, the KR580VT57 copy of the 8257 DMA controller, the KR580VN59 copy of the 8259 interrupt controller, the KR580GF24 copy of the 8224 clock generator. A complete ecosystem.

But the Soviet Union was not content with the 8080. They also wanted the Z80. Through East Germany, the U880 entered the Soviet Union. And then, Angstrem, one of the largest chip manufacturers in the Soviet Union, began producing its own version of the U880: the Т34ВМ1. Microscopic images show that the Т34ВМ1 used the same mask as the U880. That is, a copy of a copy. The Soviet Union copied from East Germany, and East Germany copied from Zilog. A long chain of technological theft.

Later, the Soviet Union produced more advanced versions as well. The KR1858VM1, in a plastic DIP-40 package, with a frequency of up to 4 MHz. And the KR1858VM3, a CMOS version with low power consumption. But the KR1858VM3 had one important difference: it executed the HALT instruction differently. It did not refresh memory. It did not increment the R register. That is, if a program waited for HALT to refresh memory, it would get stuck.

And then, perhaps the strangest part of the story: the U880 did not only stay in the East. Some of them, those that worked at a frequency of 4 MHz, were exported to the West with a Z80A label. A German engineer later revealed: "The chips were made in East Germany and tested to see if they worked at 2 or 4 MHz. If they worked at 4 MHz, the Z80A label was put on them, and they went to the West and earned foreign currency."

Those that worked only at 2 MHz remained U880s and were consumed in socialist production. Later, when the production process was optimized and all the chips worked at 4 MHz, all of them were exported to the West. Then East Germany was forced to buy the original Z80 from the West to meet domestic needs. This strange trade cost more than it earned. But this money came from one account and went to another account. And no one asked questions.

sections.title: Section Four: The Parallel World — Eastern Computers
sections.content:
With the U880 and the KR580VM80A, the Eastern Bloc could suddenly build computers. Not like the West, but enough for their needs. Enough for schools, factories, and sometimes homes.

Each Eastern Bloc country went its own way. Each chose a technological hero. Each wrote a piece of history. But in all of them, one thing was common: the heart of all these computers was the U880. The same Eastern copy of the Z80. The same chip that came out of the Karl Marx factory production line in Erfurt and traveled throughout the Eastern Bloc.

East Germany was the first and most successful Eastern Bloc country in producing Z80-based computers. They not only copied the chip, but also built a complete ecosystem of different computers: for the home, for school, for the office, and even for the arcade.

The Robotron Z1013 was introduced in 1985. A home computer sold only as a kit – a box containing an assembled and tested printed circuit board, a simple membrane keyboard, various small parts, and detailed technical documentation. Its price: 650 East German marks for the base model. About two months' salary of an average worker.

To buy a Z1013, you had to send a postcard to the Robotron shop in Erfurt. And then, you waited six to twelve months. Until one day, the postcard would return: "Come and collect your computer." Six months. Half a year. For a box of parts. But people waited. Because the Z1013 was the only computer that could be "freely" purchased in East Germany. Without needing a government permit, without needing connections. Just money, patience, and a postcard.

The Z1013 had four versions: Z1013.01 with a U880 at a frequency of 1 MHz (from second-grade chips that had failed quality tests) and 16 kilobytes of RAM, Z1013.12 with only 1 kilobyte of RAM, Z1013.16 with a U880 at 2 MHz, and Z1013.64 with 64 kilobytes of RAM. The display was only 32 by 32 characters. It had no graphics. Sound was just one simple bit. Like an intelligent typewriter. But German programmers, from these limited resources, built games. Built tools. Built software. Between late 1985 and mid-1990, around 25,000 kits were sold.

For offices, the Robotron PC 1715 came. The year 1985. A complete office computer with a large case, a 97-key keyboard with a separate numeric keypad and 15 function keys, and a monochrome display. Its heart was a U880 at a frequency of 2.25 MHz. RAM: 64 kilobytes. It had no graphics – only text. But for an East German office that wanted to type letters and manage files, it was enough.

For schools, the KC series came. The KC 85/1 with a U880 and 16 kilobytes of RAM, the KC 85/2 with 32 kilobytes, the KC 85/3 with 64 kilobytes and a powerful BASIC in ROM, and the KC 85/4 with 128 kilobytes. The KC 85/3 was installed in East German schools. Thousands of students learned BASIC with this computer.

And then, Poly-Play came – the only arcade machine built in East Germany. A large wooden box with a black-and-white display and several games. In the copy of Space Invaders, the invading flying saucers were replaced with hail clouds. The Stasi considered violent games harmful. Processor: U880. The only arcade machine a young German could find in his own city.

In the Soviet Union, the Vector-06C was born in 1987 – the graphic masterpiece of the Soviet Union. Donat Temirazov and Alexander Sokolov designed a computer that, graphically, was ahead of any Western computer of those years: 16 colors simultaneously from a palette of 256 colors, a resolution of 256 by 256 pixels. The video memory was divided into four bit planes – each pixel took its color from the combination of four bits. A KR580VM80A processor at a frequency of 3 MHz – overclocked, without an extra heatsink. RAM: 64 kilobytes, half of which was reserved for graphics. Sound: three channels. And it could run ZX Spectrum games with a software layer. Thousands of units were sold.

Poland went its own way. The Meritum I was introduced in 1983 with a German U880D and 16 kilobytes of RAM. Demand was so high that freight trailers lined up for weeks behind the factory gate. The computer, as soon as it was made, left the production line and was directly loaded onto waiting cars. No warehouse. No intermediary. Just hunger. The Meritum II came in 1985 with 48 kilobytes of RAM. The Elwro 800 Junior in 1986 – a copy of the ZX Spectrum with an original Z80A, 64 kilobytes of RAM, and Spectrum-compatible BASIC – was designed for schools.

Czechoslovakia built the Didaktik Gama. The year 1987. A copy of the ZX Spectrum with an original Z80A and the original Ferranti ULA. But it had 80 kilobytes of RAM – more than the original Spectrum. Better keyboard. Capability to connect to a monitor. It had compatibility problems – some games did not work. But for Czechoslovak schools, it was a dream. Up to 45,000 units were sold.

Romania built the CIP-03 with an original Z80A and 16 kilobytes of RAM – only for schools, with special permission. Hungary built the Microkey Primo – a computer with a Z80A that had three different modes: it could run Spectrum games, run TRS-80 programs, and connect to a Commodore 64 disk drive. One computer, three souls. For schools that could not buy all three platforms separately.

Bulgaria built the IMKO-1 and IMKO-2 with U880s for government offices. Bulgaria was the entry gate for Western technology into the Eastern Bloc – through the new Silk Road (Turkey and Greece), smuggled parts entered and were distributed to the rest of the Eastern Bloc.

sections.title: Section Five: A Different Computing Culture
sections.content:
The computer in the East was different from the West.

In the West, the computer was a commodity. You went to the store, paid money, took it home. You bought the software, or borrowed it from your friends. Thousands of magazines, thousands of books, thousands of guides. You had a choice.

In the East, however, everything was scarce. Parts, software, information, even electricity. And above all of these, the shadow of the Stasi.

In Czechoslovakia, the first personal computers were brought in through illegal trips to the West. Travel to capitalist countries was severely restricted and controlled. Nevertheless, those who succeeded hid a ZX Spectrum in their suitcase and smuggled it across the border. But the original ZX Spectrum was unimaginable for most people. An original Spectrum in the mid-1980s cost about 40,000 rubles in the Soviet Union. The average monthly salary of a Soviet worker was 250 rubles. That is, thirteen years of work, without eating or sleeping, for one computer.

So what was the solution? Copying. Copying from a copy. Copying from a copy of a copy.

The story of buying a computer in the Eastern Bloc is itself a legend. The year 1987, Prague, the shop on Spálená Street. The rumor spreads: "Tomorrow morning, fifty Didaktik Gamas are coming." At 6 in the morning, the queue is formed. Fifty people are standing. Some have come since the night before, sitting in the cold, drinking tea from flasks and waiting. The shop assistants make coffee for the tired customers. At 4:10 in the afternoon, the truck arrives. They open the boxes. They hand over the computers. Some of these machines had been reserved for their buyers years before.

In Poland, the story of the Meritum was the same. Freight trailers lined up for weeks behind the factory gate. In the Soviet Union, when the Radio-86RK kit was published in Radio magazine, readers wrote letters: "Finding parts is hard." State industries responded. Kits were produced. Factories came to the rescue. Every part that was obtained was immediately sold.

Software in the East was as scarce as hardware. Western games reached the Eastern Bloc through travelers, smugglers, and sometimes through immigrants. But even when an original cassette was found, the problem was just beginning: copy protection.

This is where the "crackers" entered the field. Crackers were programmers who broke copy protection. They altered the game code, removed the protection, and sometimes added unlimited lives or new levels to the game. And most importantly, they produced a cassette tape that anyone could copy from.

In Poland, a legend named "Bill Gilbert" – a pseudonym – began publishing a ZX Spectrum hacking manual in the mid-1980s. His group cracked games, put them on cassette, and distributed them throughout Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia. Underground shops sold cracked games at a tenth of the original price.

In Yugoslavia, groups like Futuresoft and Jansoft in the city of Ljubljana wrote their real addresses and phone numbers in magazines. The customer could call, place an order, and receive the game by mail. There was no fear of the law. Because there was no copyright law in force.

The result? A massive software smuggling network, which started in England, reached Yugoslavia, went from there to Poland and Czechoslovakia, and finally reached the Soviet Union. Each cassette was copied several times. Each copy's quality went down. Sometimes the tape was copied so many times that the game's sound was lost under the hiss of the tape. But still, the game ran.

Computer clubs, however, were under the Stasi's shadow. An internal Stasi document from November 1988 explicitly says: "Considering that among hobbyist groups or computer clubs there are members with proven negative attitudes toward the state and the socialist order, there is a potential danger that these groups will take a negative direction. Political opponents are increasingly using computers."

The same document warns about Western software: "Some owners of personal computers... engage in extensive trade of hardware and software. In many cases, the software in question are copies from the non-socialist economic area that are then distributed in East Germany."

But despite this surveillance, the clubs were not shut down. The Stasi watched, recorded, but did not interfere. Because it did not know how to interfere.

In the Soviet Union, Radio magazine – the most widely circulated electronics magazine in the Soviet Union – published the design of a computer called the Radio-86RK in 1986. Simple, cheap, buildable by amateurs. It needed only 29 chips. Nineteen of these 29 chips were just one specific model: the KR580VG75, a copy of the Intel 8275. The estimated cost of parts: 260 rubles. About one month's salary of an engineer. Expensive, but possible.

Radio magazine had opened a magic box. Anyone could go and buy the parts (if they could find them), sit down at night and solder, and become the owner of a computer. Readers wrote letters: "Finding parts is hard." The magazine wrote to Soviet industries. And the industries responded. By the end of the 1980s, Radio-86RK kits were being produced industrially. Under various names: Elektronika KR-01, KR-02, KR-03, KR-04. Kit price: 395 rubles.

This was the great difference between East and West: in the West, you bought a computer from the store. In the East, you sometimes built it yourself.

The same "do it yourself" culture that caused the personal computer revolution in the West was repeated in the East. But with less budget, with more surveillance, and with the Stasi's shadow overhead. And perhaps, this very culture of resistance was the Z80's most important achievement in the East. Not just selling chips, not just copying, not just reverse engineering. But creating a generation of engineers who knew how to build something from nothing. A generation that grew up with the Z80 at midnight, in small rooms, with smuggled cassette tapes and handmade circuits. And later, when the Wall fell, they showed the world that a technological siege can never besiege the human mind.

sections.title: Section Six: Beyond the Iron Curtain — The Sanctioned Who Found Their Own Way
sections.content:
CoCom had not only targeted the Soviet Union. There were other countries too that, outside the Eastern Bloc, were under technological sanctions – Iran after the 1979 revolution, North Korea, Cuba. For these countries, access to Western technology was even harder than for the Eastern Bloc. But technological hunger finds its own way. And the Z80, as always, passed through the cracks of sanctions.

In Iran of the 1980s, conditions were more complex than anywhere else. The country was engaged in a devastating war with Iraq, Western sanctions were becoming harsher by the day, and access to electronic components seemed almost impossible. But the Z80 opened its way to Iran – not through official contracts, but through intermediaries who accepted the risk of circumventing sanctions. From Dubai, from Turkey, through Eastern Bloc countries that were themselves under sanctions but were willing to trade with Iran. Chips were hidden in travelers' suitcases, concealed in shipments of spare parts, and passed through routes that were recorded on no official trade map.

For Iranian engineers, the Z80 was not a choice – it was a necessity. It was simple, its complete technical documentation was available (even if through hand-me-down photocopies), and most importantly, it could be obtained through unofficial channels. In the electrical engineering and computer departments of the universities of Tehran, Sharif University of Technology, and Amirkabir University, the Z80 became the main processor for teaching microprocessors. The students who later built the pillars of Iran's technology industry learned assembly programming with this very chip – on simple educational boards that they sometimes designed and assembled themselves.

In industry, the Z80 became the beating heart of industrial control systems. Variable message signs on streets and passenger terminals, fire alarm systems in large buildings, controllers for industrial machinery in factories – many of these worked with the Z80. Iran's Telecommunications Research Center designed Z80-based boards for telecommunication systems. In conditions where even telephone wire was difficult to import, Iranian engineers kept telecommunication networks running with this same small chip.

Unlike the Eastern Bloc, Iran never reached the mass production of Z80-based computers. Conditions were different – sanctions were harsher, the economy was entangled in war, and priorities lay elsewhere. The record of Iranian computers may not be numerous. But the same generation that learned programming with the Z80 in the laboratories of Sharif University, the same generation that grew up with smuggled parts and handmade boards, decades later built industries that astonished the world.

When Iranian drones took to the skies over the region, when defense systems tracked their targets with unbelievable precision, when guided missiles traversed their path with minimal error, the world asked: how have they reached this technology? The answer lay in those very laboratories of the 1980s – in those very Z80 boards that had come to life on the worn-out desks of universities. Knowledge that passes through the cracks of sanctions can become a power that changes global equations. And the Z80, on this path, was one of the first teachers.

---

The Z80 triumphed in the West because it was the best. It triumphed in the East because it was the only option. And in Iran, it triumphed because there was no path but to learn.

Neither the Berlin Wall could stop silicon, nor border guards, nor the Stasi, nor CoCom sanctions. The Z80 traveled from Silicon Valley, crossed the Atlantic Ocean, emerged from the pockets of smuggling travelers, was copied onto cassette tapes, circulated in underground clubs, passed through Iran's closed borders, and infiltrated the heart of camps the West never wanted it to reach.

Without permission. Without money. Only with thirst.

And this thirst was more important than any chip.

sections.title: Section One: The End of the 8-Bit Era
sections.content:
The Z80 sat on the throne. But no throne is eternal.

By the late 1970s, the Z80 held nearly sixty percent of the 8-bit processor market. From business computers to military systems, from arcades to industrial controllers — everything worked with the Z80. But on the horizon, a storm was coming. A storm that came not from the East, but from the heart of Silicon Valley.

The year was 1978. Intel introduced the 8086 processor — the company's first 16-bit processor. 29,000 transistors on a single chip. An address space of one megabyte — sixteen times that of the Z80. Speed of 5 to 10 MHz. And most importantly, an architecture that was destined to become the industry standard for the next four decades: x86.

But the 8086 in those years had one big problem: it was too expensive. Too complex. And it did not recognize the existing 8-bit software. The 8-bit market was still alive, and the Z80 was its king.

A year later, in 1979, Motorola introduced the 68000 — a real monster. 68,000 transistors. A 32-bit internal architecture with a 16-bit external data bus. An address space of 16 megabytes — 256 times that of the Z80. 32-bit registers, powerful instructions, and an orderly design that made programming with it a pleasure. Technically, the 68000 was better than the 8086 and anything else on the market.

Zilog had not sat idle. Faggin, who still had the taste of the Z80's victory under his tongue, knew that the 8-bit era was coming to an end. If Zilog wanted to survive, it had to build a 16-bit processor. Not just a faster Z80 — an entirely new architecture.

The Z8000 project began.

sections.title: Section Two: Z8000 — The Weapon That Arrived Too Late
sections.content:
Spring 1979. Zilog's office in Cupertino, California. Federico Faggin sat behind his desk, staring at the blueprints of a new chip. The Z8000. 17,500 transistors. 8 megabytes of address space. Frequency of 4 to 10 MHz. 83 instructions. Sixteen general-purpose 16-bit registers. Two processor modes — system and user — for memory protection. 256 interrupt vectors.

On paper, the Z8000 was better than Intel's 8086. Its architecture was more orderly — sixteen all-purpose registers that could be used for any task, unlike the 8086 whose registers each had their own specific job. Its instructions were more symmetrical. Its address space was eight times that of the 8086. Faggin and his team believed the Z8000 would do in the 16-bit market what the Z80 had done in the 8-bit market.

But three problems existed from day one.

First: timing. Intel's 8086 was a year ahead — introduced in June 1978, while the Z8000 came in 1979. A year in the semiconductor industry is a lifetime. In that same interval, Intel was giving 8086 samples to computer makers, training software developers, and most importantly, winning the market's trust.

Second: resources. Intel was a giant with thousands of engineers. Zilog was a small company with a limited team. Bernard Peuto, the chief architect of the Z8000, later said in an interview: "We were a small, skinny company that had made decisions on the Z80 and turned it into a great success. Now we were facing two companies that were far bigger than us — Intel and Motorola. We had no chance."

Peuto held a PhD from Berkeley and had worked at Zilog since 1976. He had designed the Z8000 architecture from scratch — not based on the Z80, but as a completely new processor. A decision that later became the Z8000's greatest weakness.

Third: incompatibility. The Z8000 was not compatible with the Z80. None of the software written for the Z80 — the entire CP/M empire, thousands of business programs, games, tools — would work on the Z8000. Faggin, the very man who had found the secret of the Z80's success in compatibility with the 8080, had this time forgotten his own lesson. He confessed years later in an interview: "Backward compatibility was the key to the Z80's success. We forgot this lesson with the Z8000. We wanted to build a new architecture, but in doing so, we lost the entire Z80 user base."

The reality was this: customers had invested millions of dollars in Z80 software. If they wanted to migrate to the Z8000, they would have to rewrite everything from scratch. And at the same time, Intel's 8086 was gradually building its own ecosystem — with MS-DOS, with business programs, with development tools.

sections.title: Section Three: Shima and the Method That Was Both Savior and Obstacle
sections.content:
In Zilog's design room, Masatoshi Shima was responsible for the physical implementation of the Z8000. The same silent and precise engineer who had turned the Z80 from paper into silicon. The same man who bent over the light table at night and placed transistors one by one.

Shima had his own particular method. He designed at the transistor level, not at the level of logic gates. His schematics were hard to read — no one else but himself could continue the design from them. But the result was the most optimized layout possible. Every transistor sat exactly where it should sit. No space was wasted.

Before the design went to silicon, Shima would build the entire circuit with TTL chips on a breadboard and test it. This was almost unprecedented in the industry — all other companies used software simulation. But Shima did not trust simulation. He wanted to see the circuit in the real world, with an oscilloscope, with a logic probe, with his own hands.

This method had worked with the Z80, because the Z80 was a relatively simple architecture evolved from the 8080. But the Z8000 was far more complex. 83 instructions, 256 interrupt vectors, two processor modes, advanced memory management — and all of this without microcode, only with hardware logic. Faggin admired Shima's method: "From an implementation perspective, he was a genius. I had never seen anyone like him." But this very method had slowed Zilog down.

At the same time, Intel and Motorola were using automated design tools — software that optimized transistor placement, calculated connection paths, and found design errors before fabrication. Zilog worked by hand — and with love. It worked. But late.

The Z8000 was finally ready in 1979. But by then, Intel's 8086 had been on the market for a year. And Motorola's 68000 was also on its way.

sections.title: Section Four: The Mortal Wound — The IBM PC
sections.content:
The year 1981 arrived. And with it, the moment that changed everything.

IBM — the largest and most prestigious computer company in the world — decided to enter the personal computer market. Until then, IBM had only built big computers. Computers whose price exceeded that of a house. But the market was changing. Altair, Apple, Tandy, Commodore — all were building small, cheap computers that ordinary people could buy. IBM did not want to be left out of this market.

The IBM PC project was executed in the fastest possible time — just one year from design to production. For the first time in its history, IBM used standard off-the-shelf components instead of its own proprietary parts. And for the heart of the machine, it needed a processor.

Three options were on the table: the Intel 8086, the Motorola 68000, and the Zilog Z8000.

The 68000 was not ready — the 8-bit bus version needed to reduce cost was still under design. The Z8000 was ready — but IBM did not choose it. Why?

There is an old rumor in the industry that says Exxon — the oil giant that was now the main owner of Zilog — was at that time competing with IBM in the word processing business. IBM did not want to give money to its competitor for the processor. Joseph Fernandez, former head of Zilog, later said in an interview with the Computer History Museum: "Some say the reason IBM did not choose the Z8000 was because Exxon owned most of Zilog. Exxon was directly competing with IBM in the word processing business. They didn't want to have any part of it."

Bernard Peuto had a similar view: "IBM could invest in Intel, but because of Exxon they could not invest in Zilog."

Whatever the truth — Exxon's competition, or perhaps simply IBM's conservatism, or perhaps the Z8000's higher price, or perhaps the lack of sufficient software — the result was one: IBM chose the Intel 8088 processor. The cheaper version of the 8086 that had an 8-bit data bus and was compatible with the market's low-cost peripheral components.

The IBM PC was introduced in August 1981. And it changed the world.

Sales of the IBM PC exceeded all predictions. Companies, offices, banks — all were buying IBM. IBM meant trust. IBM meant standard. And the standard was the 8088.

The market turned overnight toward the x86 architecture. Not because x86 was better — because IBM had chosen it. Stores sold IBM and IBM-compatible computers. Programmers wrote software for MS-DOS. Companies bought IBM software. And the Z8000, however technically good it was, remained outside this ecosystem.

The Z8000 did not fail — but it did not triumph either. In the high end, Motorola's 68000 crushed it. The Apple Macintosh used the 68000 — a computer that shook the world in 1984 with the famous "1984" advertisement. The Atari ST, the Amiga, and Sun Microsystems also chose the 68000. The 68000 ruled in workstations, in graphics computers, in multimedia systems.

In the low and middle market, Intel's 8086 and 8088 and then the 80286 were victorious. The IBM PC and its clones — Compaq, Dell, HP — all with x86. Software was written for x86. Peripheral cards were built for x86. Books and magazines were about x86.

The Z8000 had no place in this middle. It was not powerful enough to compete with the 68000. It was not cheap enough to fight the 8086. And most importantly, it was not compatible. Old Z80 customers could not migrate to the Z8000. And new customers preferred x86 or the 68000.

The Olivetti M20 from Italy used the Z8000 — but had limited sales. The Commodore 900, a workstation with two Z8000s, came to market but quickly vanished. A few telecommunications and military systems also chose the Z8000 — places where software compatibility did not matter and the Z8000's processing power was useful. But these markets were not large enough to keep Zilog alive.

sections.title: Section Five: The Collapse of the Dream Team
sections.content:
By 1978, a year before the Z8000's launch, internal disputes at Zilog had reached their peak. Ralph Ungermann — the clever executive who had stood beside Faggin from day one and designed the market map — ran into trouble with Exxon.

Exxon had injected a lot of money into Zilog. And too much money is sometimes worse than too little. Bernard Peuto later said: "Exxon smothered us with money. They gave us too much money and set too many directions. Sometimes you had to say no, but when someone gives you money, saying no is very hard."

Ungermann left the company. He later founded Ungermann-Bass — a company in the networking industry that itself became a great success. After that, he built Bridge Communications. Ungermann remained in the networking industry for years to come. But he never returned to the world of microprocessors.

Faggin stayed. Shima stayed. But the atmosphere of the company was no longer like the early days. The three who had decided to found Zilog in that Santa Clara restaurant were now either gone or on the verge of leaving. That small office in Los Altos, with the metal desks and graph paper and the smell of midnight coffee — no longer existed. Now Zilog was a big company, with big investors, with bureaucracy, with endless meetings.

In 1980, Masatoshi Shima decided to return to Japan.

The man whose hands had turned the Z80 from paper into silicon, the man who had embedded six traps in the design to fool Japanese copiers, the man who bent over the light table at night and placed transistors one by one — was going home.

He founded Intel's design center in Japan. He was no longer the young engineer who had come from Busicom to Intel, gone from Intel to Zilog, and made history with Faggin. Now he was a manager. A professor. Years later, at the University of Aizu, he taught Japanese students computer architecture. His pupils did not know that behind the desk sat a man whose hand had touched the silicon of the first microprocessors in history. A man without whom neither the 4004 would have been built, nor the 8080, nor the Z80.

Shima was inducted into the Computer History Museum in 2009. He also received the Kyoto Prize — together with Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin, and Stanley Mazor. The four who changed the world. But he was never, like Faggin, one for interviews. Always silent. Always humble. Always in the shadows. He retired in 2004. But his footprint on the Z80 remained forever.

In 1982, Faggin also left Zilog.

The man who had come from Fairchild to Intel to build the 4004, the man who had designed the 8080 and then founded Zilog to prove he could be better than everyone, the man who had built the Z80 from nothing and conquered the world with it — was leaving.

He founded Synaptics. The company that later built the touchpads for laptops — again a revolution, again a new industry. Faggin never stopped innovating.

But he did not forget the Z80. Years later, in an interview, when asked if the Z8000 had failed, he said: "We didn't want to build a better processor. We wanted to build the last processor. The last processor anyone would need for ordinary tasks besides anything else."

The Z8000 was not the last. The last was the Z80 itself.

Bernard Peuto also left Zilog. He went to Sun Microsystems, where he led the SPARC graphics team. In 2019, in San Francisco, he passed away from injuries sustained in a car accident years earlier.

The three musketeers of silicon — Faggin, Ungermann, Shima — and the architect of the Z8000 — Peuto — each scattered in a different direction. But what they had built was going its own way. Independent of them. Alive.

sections.title: Section Six: Life in the Shadows — The Hidden Generations of the Z80
sections.content:
While the Z8000 fought and lost against the 68000 and the 8086, the Z80 quietly went about its work. The 8-bit market had not died — it had only changed shape.

The cheap home computers of the 1980s — the Spectrum, the Amstrad CPC, MSX — sold millions of machines, all with the Z80. The graphing calculators from Texas Instruments — TI-81, TI-82, TI-83, TI-84 — used by millions of students in math classes, all worked with the Z80. ATMs, industrial controllers, telecommunications equipment, fax machines, modems, fire alarm systems, variable message signs — all with the Z80.

The Nintendo Game Boy, introduced in 1989 and becoming one of the best-selling consoles in history, had a copy of the Z80 as its heart — made by Sharp, under the name LR35902. The same architecture, the same instructions, the same soul. Millions of children around the world spent hours with a device whose pulse beat to the rhythm of the Z80.

And the Z80 evolved.

Hitachi built the HD64180 — a supercharged Z80 with advanced memory management that could address up to one megabyte of memory. Two DMA channels for fast data transfer. Two serial ports. An internal timer. And all of this while maintaining full compatibility with the Z80. Zilog sent this chip to market under the name Z180, and it was used in embedded systems, industrial controllers, and telecommunications equipment for decades.

Then came the Z280 — a more powerful version with cache memory, a floating-point unit, and a speed several times that of the original Z80. The Z280 could compete with 16-bit processors while still running old Z80 software.

And finally, the eZ80 — the modern version of the Z80 introduced in the 2000s. Frequency up to 50 MHz. Address space of 16 megabytes. Ability to run real-time operating systems. The eZ80 was used in routers, in network equipment, in modern industrial control systems. The Z80 had not died — it had only changed.

But it was no longer in the shop window. It was inside devices. In places no one looked. In millions of embedded systems that worked silently and on which no one saw the Z80 name.

sections.title: Section Seven: The Last Breath
sections.content:
And then, the news came.

The year 2024. Zilog announced it was discontinuing production of the Z80.

After forty-eight years.

Forty-eight years from that night in Los Altos when Faggin said: "It is finished. We have it." Forty-eight years from that day when Shima, with trembling hands, placed the chip in the socket and the oscilloscope screen began to wave. Forty-eight years from that moment when the Z80 beat its first pulses in the real world.

In these forty-eight years, Intel's 4004 and 8008 and 8080 and 8085 had passed into history. The 6800 and 6502 too. The 8086 and 80286 and 80386 and 80486 too. Pentium and Pentium II and Pentium III too. Generations of processors had come and gone — but the Z80 was still there.

It was still on the production line. It still had orders. It still breathed in the devices we used every day.

And now, after nearly half a century, Zilog had said: it is finished. The last wafers had left the production line. The last chips had been packaged and shipped. The last orders had been recorded.

The semiconductor industry, of which the Z80 was one of the founders, no longer needed it. ARM and x86 and RISC-V had conquered the world. The Z80 was a retiree — the oldest retiree of Silicon Valley.

But the Z80 did not die. Like a stubborn old man sitting in a storeroom and breathing, it remained in industrial controllers. In old devices that still worked. In museums. In the collections of enthusiasts. In the memories of a generation that had written the first computer program of their lives with the Z80.

And in the hearts of engineers who had grown up with it and were now designing the next generation of chips.

sections.title: Section Eight: Epilogue
sections.content:
I grew up with the Amiga.

It was winter. I was supposed to buy a ZX Spectrum 48K a year before. For two years I had been seeing this small and mysterious system in the room of one of my friends, and I still remember the gleam that appeared in my friend's eyes when touching the soft keyboard of the machine. The very computer you read about in the third chapter of this book, with the rubber keyboard and cassette tapes that took five minutes to load. It did not happen.

Destiny placed a Commodore 64 in my hands instead of a Spectrum. And the course of my life changed forever.

But that Commodore was only the beginning. A year later, the Amiga 500 arrived, and the year after that, the Amiga 600. I still have it, and for more than thirty years, I have lived with this machine. The Amiga was not just a computer. It was a world. A world with 4096 simultaneous colors and smooth animations and stereo sound pouring out of four digital channels. A world in which the boundary between computer and art disappeared. A place where the programmer and the painter and the musician were all one person.

This long life alongside the Amiga gradually turned me into something more than a user. It turned me into a narrator of these machines. For years I wrote about Commodore and Amiga, on a blog I named after that old love, and in a book I wrote some time ago called "The Amazing Computers of the 1980s." In Iran, for more than a decade, I have been writing in the small but passionate world of retro computers — perhaps more than anyone else in the Persian language. Narrating the history of these machines is itself a form of immortality — a way to ensure that those days, those colors, those sounds, are never completely silenced.

But there was always a question in the corner of my mind: what was on the other side?

If that winter, the Spectrum had come into my hands, what would have happened? If instead of the visual world of the Amiga, I had sunk into the hardware world of the Z80 — into that orderly and unadorned architecture, into those dual registers and block instructions, into that world where everything had to be built with 8 bits and every byte of memory had to be preserved like gold — where would my life's path have ended? Would there even have been a narrator? Or would I myself have become part of that history?

This book is the answer to that very question.

Not for comparison with Commodore. Not to prove the superiority of one over the other. For respect. To pay homage to the path I did not take. To understand what was happening on the other side of the wall — how an 8-bit chip, without an army of engineers, without billion-dollar budgets, without flashy advertising, managed to endure for forty-eight years.

And I understood.

That the Z80 did not win because it was the best — though at its peak, it was the most powerful of all. It did not win because it was the fastest — though its 4 MHz frequency was dazzling in its time. The Z80 won because it was accessible. Because it was simple. Because it was cheap. Because engineers could build a complete system around it with the fewest peripheral components. Because its documentation was complete. Because a student in Brazil could learn programming with a copy of the Spectrum. Because an engineer in East Germany could build his own version from smuggled circuits. Because a university professor in Tehran could teach the next generation with chips that had reached the country through a thousand secret paths.

The Z80 was the story of ordinary people — those who, with the fewest resources, showed the greatest creativity.

From Silicon Valley to Tokyo, from London to Moscow, from São Paulo to Tehran. The Z80 was everywhere. In American submarines and Japanese arcades. In Manchester bedrooms and São Paulo workshops. In the laboratories of Iranian universities and East German schools. In fax machines and pocket calculators and Game Boys that entertained millions of children.

Wherever there was a computer, somewhere a Z80 was breathing.

And now, after forty-eight years, its breaths were numbered.

I, as someone who has lived with Commodore and Amiga — and as someone who has spent years narrating the history of these machines — today take my hat off to the Z80. To Federico Faggin who saw his dream. To Masatoshi Shima who turned it into silicon with his own hands. To Ralph Ungermann who drew its market map. To that eleven-person team in the small office in Los Altos who, with a meager budget, wrote history. To the engineers who wove dreams with it in garages and workshops. To the generation that grew up with it and then changed the world.

Z80, you fought well.

Now rest.
